docs.t: CLM-000280 Eli Lilly TuneLab Catalyze360 federated learning data_ai partnerships_ma competitive_advantage

Access is federated (third-party hosted) and partners contribute training data in return. An ecosystem/platform move: Lilly offers proprietary models to biotechs in exchange for data contributions (data-for-access), analogous in intent to developer-platform strategies. The corpus shows no revenue or asset outcome from TuneLab; whether it yields assets is unproven.

docs.t: CLM-000281 Eli Lilly NVIDIA BioNeMo autonomous laboratory data_ai robotics_automation partnerships_ma

docs.t: CLM-000286 Eli Lilly Johnson & Johnson AbbVie data_ai robotics_automation competitive_advantage
docs.x: Across the three competitors' most recent technology announcements, only OTTAVA has a regulator-verified milestone (FDA De Novo) and a commercial installation; Lilly's TuneLab is a live platform without disclosed scientific outcomes; the NVIDIA–Lilly lab and the AbbVie–Valkai partnership are announcements with no reported deployment metrics. docs.t: CLM-006000 State of Indiana advanced manufacturing process development robotics_automation
docs.x: On 2024-10-02 Lilly announced a USD 4.5 billion Lilly Medicine Foundry in Lebanon, Indiana, a facility combining process research and clinical-supply manufacturing, with opening stated as late 2027, about 400 planned jobs, and technologies developed there to be transferred to Lilly's other sites. Capital commitment, not an operating capability; automation scope of the Foundry is not described in the release.

docs.t: CLM-006001 robotics_automation
docs.x: As of the 6 May 2026 opening of Lilly Lebanon Advanced Therapies, local press reported the Lilly Medicine Foundry and the Lilly Lebanon API site were still planned, with the API site due to open in 2027.

docs.t: CLM-006002 robotics_automation
docs.x: On 2026-05-06 Lilly opened its Lilly Lebanon Advanced Therapies genetic-medicine plant and announced a further USD 4.5 billion for the Lebanon campus (more than USD 21 billion of Indiana commitments since 2020); a reporter on the guided tour saw staff monitoring robotic machines that dose, measure and seal medicines. Evidence that robotic fill-finish-type equipment is installed at a newly opened Lilly site; effect on cost or cycle time is not measured.

docs.t: CLM-006003 NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD B300 BioNeMo Omniverse Isaac data_ai
docs.x: At NVIDIA GTC Washington, D.C. in October 2025, NVIDIA and Lilly announced a Lilly 'AI factory' built as an NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD with DGX B300 systems and 1,016 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, rated at over 9,000 petaflops of AI performance, to train biomedical foundation models. Compute is purchased, replicable by competitors with capital; differentiation depends on data and models, not the cluster.

docs.t: CLM-006004 NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD Spectrum-X data_ai
docs.x: Lilly's AI supercomputer, branded LillyPod, was inaugurated at a ribbon-cutting in Indianapolis (reported late February 2026), assembled in about four months, with over 9,000 petaflops, 700 TB of genomics data and over 290 TB of GPU memory, and a stated target of 100% renewable electricity by 2030. Infrastructure is online; no disclosed model released from it or scientific result attributable to it.

docs.t: CLM-006005 data_ai
docs.x: Lilly's VP of R&D informatics said that productive teams typically analyse roughly 2,000 molecular ideas per target per year because each needs physical synthesis and testing, and that the supercomputer lets scientists evaluate billions of molecular hypotheses computationally before wet-lab work. The throughput claim is about candidate generation; the binding constraint (experimental validation) is unchanged until the wet-lab loop is automated.

docs.t: CLM-006006 digital twin NVIDIA Isaac Omniverse robotics_automation
docs.x: NVIDIA's October 2025 blog states Lilly uses robots in its factories for quality inspection and transport of goods and plans digital twins of manufacturing lines on NVIDIA Omniverse; it gives no deployment counts, sites or results. Manufacturing digital twins and robots are asserted but unevidenced beyond one vendor article; 10-K (CLM-000252) quantifies none.

docs.t: CLM-006007 data_ai
docs.x: No source opened for this review reports a scientific, cycle-time or financial outcome attributable to the Lilly AI factory or the planned NVIDIA co-innovation lab as of 2026-11-21. Treat Lilly's AI infrastructure as a capability bet whose value is unproven; revisit after Lilly's next R&D day or model releases via TuneLab.

docs.t: CLM-006008 Benchling NVIDIA FLARE federated learning data_ai
docs.x: On 2026-01-08 Benchling announced it would distribute Lilly TuneLab antibody and small-molecule prediction models to its more than 1,300 biotech customers, with customers able to opt in 'later this year'; no uptake figures were given. Reach is being built through third-party platforms where biotech scientists already work; participation numbers remain undisclosed.

docs.t: CLM-006009 insitro ADMET prediction federated learning data_ai
docs.x: On 2025-09-09 insitro announced a collaboration to build machine-learning models predicting small-molecule ADMET and in vivo behaviour from Lilly's proprietary preclinical data, with the models to be available through Lilly TuneLab; it expands a 2024 insitro-Lilly relationship on siRNA delivery and antibody discovery.

docs.t: CLM-006010 Chai Discovery data_ai
docs.x: BiopharmaTrend reported in early 2026 that Chai Discovery and Lilly agreed to build a custom antibody-design model on Lilly's proprietary data, with no financial terms disclosed; the reported double-digit zero-shot hit rate for Chai-2 is Chai's own claim. Lilly is buying access to several external model builders in parallel (insitro, Chai, Isomorphic, OpenAI).

docs.t: CLM-006011 OpenAI data_ai
docs.x: On 2024-06-25 Lilly announced a collaboration with OpenAI to use generative AI to invent novel antimicrobials against drug-resistant pathogens; the release states no financial terms, targets, timelines or results.

docs.t: CLM-006012 Isomorphic Labs AlphaFold partnerships_ma
docs.x: On 2024-01-07 Isomorphic Labs announced a multi-target small-molecule collaboration with Lilly: USD 45 million upfront, up to USD 1.7 billion in performance-based milestones, and tiered royalties up to low double digits. Option-style economics: cash at risk is the USD 45 million upfront; no candidate has been disclosed in the sources reviewed.

docs.t: CLM-006013 Arctoris Strateos cloud lab robotic automation robotics_automation
docs.x: In 2024 (reported September) Arctoris acquired Lilly's Life Sciences Studio automated laboratory, relocating the platform from San Diego to Oxford and adding five automated biochemistry modules, a high-throughput screening module, a BSL2 cell-biology module and storage for 4 million compounds. A pharma-built open robotic lab was handed to an external CRO four years after launch.

docs.t: CLM-006014 robotics_automation
docs.x: BiopharmaTrend states the Life Sciences Studio was established by Lilly in 2017 as part of a USD 90 million investment; a Fierce Biotech snippet describes the lab as launched four years before the 2024 sale, which conflicts with a 2017 start. Cost figure is unverified; treat as an order of magnitude.

docs.t: CLM-006015 robotics_automation
docs.x: An aggregator profile (not opened; search snippet only) reports that Strateos, Lilly's robotic cloud-lab partner, was acquired by Multiply Labs in December 2023; no primary announcement was found and the research brief's 'Strateos closed 2023' framing is not confirmed as a closure. If confirmed, Strateos ended as an independent company via acquisition by a robotic-manufacturing firm, not an outright shutdown.

docs.t: CLM-006016 Arctoris ARIA robotics_automation
docs.x: By March 2026 Arctoris described the ex-Lilly platform as part of a cloud-controlled robotic system running biochemistry, biophysics, cell-biology and structural-biology workflows, announced a ten-fold biophysics instrumentation expansion, and said it was selected for the UK ARIA AI Scientist programme targeting endometriosis. The asset survives in a service (CRO) model that sells experimental data to many AI-drug-discovery customers rather than serving one pharma.

docs.t: CLM-006017 robotics_automation
docs.x: The Lilly-Strateos remote robotic laboratory (public launch about 2020) no longer operates under Lilly: its hardware was divested to a CRO in 2024. The reason is undisclosed, so the sources support a retreat from an owned open cloud lab but not a cause. Calibration for Takeda: owning an open-access robotic lab did not keep it inside Lilly; renting from a CRO preserves optionality.

docs.t: CLM-006018 data_ai
docs.x: In a March 2025 interview J&J's CIO said J&J had reviewed nearly 900 generative-AI use cases for ethical, regulatory and compliance risk, that much of the prior two years' gen-AI work had been proofs of concept and pilots, and that the company was now deploying gen AI. J&J describes a funnel from hundreds of pilots to a focused set of deployments; the number deployed is not given.

docs.t: CLM-006019 data_ai
docs.x: J&J's CIO said (as relayed by The Batch, citing Greylock and The Wall Street Journal) that 10-15% of use cases drove about 80% of the value, after which J&J moved responsibility for AI projects to departments to focus on high-value applications. Evidence of portfolio pruning discipline rather than an outcome.

docs.t: CLM-006020 data_ai
docs.x: J&J's CIO said AI models recommending clinical-trial sites produced 'up to a 2.6x increase in enrollment' at better-performing, higher-enrolling recommended sites; the baseline, method and trials are not disclosed. Plausible mechanism (site selection) but unverified magnitude; do not treat as a demonstrated outcome.

docs.t: CLM-006021 data_ai
docs.x: J&J's CIO said a gen-AI tool launched in quality control lets service representatives answer product-identification and regulatory questions across hundreds of thousands of SKUs in minutes instead of weeks.

docs.t: CLM-006022 data_ai
docs.x: J&J's CIO reported more than 30,000 completions of its 'digital boot camp' courses and 47,000 employees completing a required generative-AI course, from a workforce of more than 130,000.

docs.t: CLM-006023 data_ai
docs.x: J&J's CIO named AI tools in use or deployed: a sales-rep assistant (AskJIA), an engagement tool (Engagement.AI) used for provider insights in over 14 countries, a supply-risk sensing platform, and an HR service agent; no usage or outcome data accompany them.

docs.t: CLM-006024 scientific_rd
docs.x: J&J's CIO said AI-powered image analytics on its biosignature platform helped J&J deliver novel molecular entities 'faster than we would have been able to before'; no counts, timelines or comparison are given. Cannot be tested from public data; ask J&J for candidate counts and cycle times.

docs.t: CLM-006025 data_ai
docs.x: J&J's FY2025 10-K says J&J uses data science, machine learning and other AI across parts of its business and warns that its AI investments may not deliver a competitive advantage or may become obsolete (line 428); it quantifies no AI outcome, and its text contains no references to OTTAVA or MONARCH. Investors receive no robotics installed-base or AI value disclosure in the 10-K.

docs.t: CLM-006026 robotics_automation
docs.x: J&J's FY2025 10-K attributes growth in Knees to the ATTUNE portfolio and 'pull through related to the VELYS Robotic assisted solution' but reports no VELYS system or procedure counts. Robotics matters commercially as a pull-through for implants; ask for installed base.

docs.t: CLM-006027 MONARCH QUEST 3 nodule segmentation CBCT robotics_automation
docs.x: On 2026-08-17 J&J announced 510(k) clearance for MONARCH QUEST 3 software adding AI-powered nodule segmentation, registration and navigation improvements, a 3D Compass overlay and broader CBCT compatibility, and said it followed three launches in 18 months; supporting design evidence cited is internal technical reviews. MONARCH is a mature, iterating software-defined platform (first flexible robotic bronchoscopy system per the release); AI is incremental inside a cleared device.

docs.t: CLM-006028 OTTAVA robotics_automation
docs.x: J&J says OTTAVA has four arms integrated into the operating table and, in its IDE trial, fitted operating rooms as small as 243 sq ft (five of six trial ORs previously non-robotic); a user-experience survey behind its efficiency claims covered 12 surgeons and 8 staff after 1-5 gastric bypass cases each. Differentiation is a footprint and table-integrated architecture; efficiency benefit unproven at scale.

docs.t: CLM-006029 robotics_automation
docs.x: As of 2026-11-19 OTTAVA has FDA De Novo authorization (2026-07-22, CLM-000283) and one announced commercial installation (CLM-000284), with J&J giving no revenue, unit-sale, order-book or procedure data. Commercial maturity is at launch; compare with Intuitive and Medtronic before assuming competitiveness.

docs.t: CLM-006030 NVIDIA AWS Mayo Clinic Polyphonic data_ai
docs.x: J&J said on 2025-10-27 that its Polyphonic digital ecosystem 'is available in early access to select hospitals only', and that the first Polyphonic AI Fund QuickFire Challenge drew entries from 29 countries and awarded Mayo Clinic and QAS.AI. Surgical-data network is pre-scale; value depends on hospitals contributing video data.

docs.t: CLM-006031 Abu Dhabi DOH AWS NVIDIA data_ai
docs.x: On 2026-05-21 J&J announced a programme with the Abu Dhabi Department of Health under which Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, PureHealth, Mediclinic and NMC Healthcare are to deploy Polyphonic across operating rooms, creating a governed anonymised surgical-data source for AI development; the release says deployment is 'expected'. A government-sponsored data node could give J&J a durable surgical-video dataset; not yet realised.

docs.t: CLM-006032 Modak SciBite Tellic TXI Digital Cloudera knowledge graph NLP data_ai
docs.x: At Bio-IT World in 2023 AbbVie's head of AI said the AbbVie R&D Convergence Hub (ARCH), conceived in 2020, was built by fewer than ten full-time AbbVie staff plus many contractors (Modak, SciBite, Tellic, TXI), harmonised a corpus over 124 TB, and exposes a graph of over 30 million nodes and nearly 2 billion relationships to all R&D employees. ARCH is a knowledge-graph and data-governance asset; the source does not describe it as a generative-AI platform, contrary to the research brief.

docs.t: CLM-006033 data_ai

No outcome beyond a preprint; cost undisclosed. Value case rests on productivity and data reuse.

docs.t: CLM-006034 data_ai

The enabling asset is the governance decision to open trial data internally, which is replicable but organisationally hard.

docs.t: CLM-006043 Apheris OpenFold3 AISB-1-Fed data_ai
docs.x: Apheris states that five companies (AbbVie, Astex, BMS, J&J, Takeda) jointly fine-tuned OpenFold3 in under ten weeks on over 20,000 private structures, outperforming every public model tested by about 10 points on pose accuracy and 11 points on interface quality on 1,056 held-out private structures; results are not peer-reviewed. Concrete evidence that a multi-pharma federated model can beat public models on drug-like complexes, subject to independent confirmation.

docs.t: CLM-006044 data_ai

Takeda is absent from the next-stage binding consortium as listed; a watch item.

docs.t: CLM-006045 data_ai
docs.x: Takeda's 20-F lists digital transformation and AI integration as initiatives and risk factors with no quantified AI outcome (CLM-000278), and none of the Takeda sources opened in this review reports a named, internally deployed AI system with metrics. Takeda's disclosed AI posture is external partnering; baseline depth only.

docs.t: CLM-006046 policy_regulation

docs.t: CLM-006047 successes_failures

AI-platform origin did not protect clinical programmes from ordinary attrition.

docs.t: CLM-006048 successes_failures
docs.x: A June 2025 Nature Medicine Phase IIa study (71 IPF patients, 12 weeks) of AI-discovered rentosertib showed +98.4 mL mean FVC at 60 mg versus -20.3 mL on placebo, with seven discontinuations for liver injury or dysfunction and 67% completion of the high-dose arm versus 88% on placebo, as reported by Drug Discovery Trends. Best public yardstick that a fully AI-originated target and molecule can show Phase IIa signal; far from approval.

docs.t: CLM-006049 successes_failures
docs.x: Drug Discovery Trends cites prior analyses that AI-originated compounds clear Phase 2 at about the same 40% rate as conventional drugs and lists discontinued Exscientia (EXS-21546) and BenevolentAI (BEN-2293) programmes. No evidence yet of a higher clinical success rate for AI-originated molecules.

docs.t: CLM-006050 scientific_rd

docs.t: CLM-006051 Ginkgo Bioworks biofoundry automation robotics_automation
docs.x: Ginkgo Bioworks agreed in July 2022 to buy Zymergen for about USD 300 million, one-tenth of its roughly USD 3 billion valuation at its April 2021 IPO, after Zymergen reported cumulative net losses of USD 1.2 billion, discontinued its first product, and had cut 220 jobs with 80 more planned. Highly automated, ML-driven biofoundry did not deliver commercial products at the scale priced into its IPO.

docs.t: CLM-006052 robotics_automation
docs.x: Across the cases reviewed, the owned or venture-funded 'cloud lab' and biofoundry models (Lilly Life Sciences Studio, Zymergen) ended in divestment or distressed sale, while the service-lab model continues at a CRO (Arctoris); no fully autonomous closed-loop lab with a published discovery outcome was found in any source opened. Treat 'autonomous lab' as early-stage; buy data generation as a service.

docs.t: CLM-006053 competitive_advantage
docs.x: Lilly has the most aggressive AI build (own compute, a data-as-product platform, many external model partners), J&J concentrates on productivity use cases plus MedTech robotics and surgical data, AbbVie on an internal knowledge graph plus partners, and Takeda on external partnerships.

docs.t: CLM-006054 competitive_advantage
docs.x: Only J&J's MedTech devices have regulator-verified and commercial milestones (OTTAVA De Novo, MONARCH 510(k) iterations); no source opened shows a published discovery outcome, cost saving or revenue effect from any of the four companies' AI drug-discovery or data initiatives. Maturity is dominated by announcements and infrastructure; Takeda should not infer competitor advantage from announcement volume.

docs.t: CLM-006055 competitive_advantage
docs.x: Lilly's most defensible asset is proprietary experimental data (company-estimated over USD 1 billion to generate, CLM-000280) paired with a federated platform that lets partners add data; compute and third-party models are purchasable by rivals. Replicating needs decades of consistent assay data, which Takeda may not have in comparable volume.

docs.t: CLM-006056 data_ai
docs.x: Both Lilly TuneLab and the Apheris AISB consortium use federated learning so partners can improve shared models without pooling raw data; TuneLab is Lilly-led and AISB is multi-pharma, with Takeda, AbbVie and J&J in AISB. Federated models are the emerging route for smaller data holders such as Takeda.

docs.t: CLM-006057 financials
docs.x: Disclosed cash costs of the AI programmes are limited to deal terms (Isomorphic USD 45 million upfront, BigHat USD 30 million, Nabla double-digit millions, Iambic unspecified), the unquantified ARCH investment, a USD 1 billion co-innovation lab (CLM-000281) and a USD 90 million legacy lab figure. Return on AI spend cannot be computed from public data.

docs.t: CLM-006058 strategy
docs.x: Takeda should prioritise partner-and-watch moves: continue federated consortia (AISB), use contract automation rather than build an owned robotic lab, and require Nabla/Iambic go/no-go gates tied to first-in-human data before scaling spend; matching Lilly's compute build is not supported by the evidence.

docs.t: CLM-006059 strategy
docs.x: Takeda should watch four triggers: independent scientific outputs from Lilly's TuneLab and LillyPod, OTTAVA commercial uptake data, the Nabla first-in-human readout, and whether AISB expands beyond structure prediction without Takeda.

docs.t: CLM-009095 partnerships_ma
docs.x: Lilly's window deals split into early-stage asset purchases expensed as IPR&D (DICE $1.9B, Morphic $2.5B, Scorpion $1.4B, Versanis $0.6B, SiteOne $0.5B, Emergence $0.4B), capability purchases as business combinations (POINT, Verve, Akouos, NexPharm) and a 2025-26 platform layer (TuneLab, NVIDIA). Lilly pairs many Phase 1-2 asset buys with a platform ecosystem; no window-acquired asset was approved at cutoff in the sources reviewed.

docs.t: CLM-009096 partnerships_ma
docs.x: J&J's window moves from mid-size bolt-ons to a few large commercial or late-stage acquisitions (Abiomed $17.1B, Shockwave $11.5B, Intra-Cellular $14.5B), plus smaller platform buys (Ambrx, Halda, Proteologix). Revenue-producing targets cut pipeline-failure risk but concentrate dollars in three deals.

docs.t: CLM-009097 partnerships_ma
docs.x: AbbVie's window combines two large purchases (ImmunoGen $9.2B net, Cerevel $8.3B net) with a steady stream of $130M-$2.1B early-stage asset buys and option licences and an annual $0.6-1.0B 'other' upfront stream. AbbVie is the most deal-intense and had the largest single write-off (emraclidine).

docs.t: CLM-009098 partnerships_ma
docs.x: Takeda's window has one flagship asset purchase (Nimbus, $4.0B upfront plus $2.0B sales milestones), then licences and options (Protagonist, Keros, Innovent, Ascentage), divestitures, and write-offs of earlier purchases (Maverick, soticlestat, gamma delta T-cell). Licences and options limit upfront cash at risk after Nimbus.

docs.t: CLM-009099 partnerships_ma
docs.x: Contingent value rights appear in Lilly's Prevail, Akouos and Verve deals and J&J's Abiomed deal; AbbVie and Takeda use contingent consideration or sales milestones (Nimble, DJS, Nimbus). Deferred value cuts upfront risk but did not prevent later write-downs (Prevail GBA1).

docs.t: CLM-009100 successes_failures
docs.x: Audited write-downs tied to window-era purchases include AbbVie emraclidine $4.5B, J&J Ottava $0.9B and bermekimab $0.8B, Lilly GBA1 gene therapy (2022 charges $244.6M) and Vitrakvi, and Takeda JPY 58.2B (gamma delta T-cell), JPY 27.8B (Maverick), JPY 21.5B (soticlestat). Neuroscience and novel-modality purchases (gene therapy, cell therapy, robotics) account for most disclosed value destruction.

docs.t: CLM-009101 data_ai
docs.x: Evidenced ecosystem arms are Lilly's Catalyze360/TuneLab/NVIDIA, J&J's JLABS/JJDC, Takeda's Center for External Innovation (BaseLaunch) and AbbVie Ventures; only Lilly's TuneLab and NVIDIA involve data or compute exchange rather than capital or incubation. Lilly is the only one of the four with documented data-for-access and compute alliances.

docs.t: CLM-001000 financials
docs.x: In FY2021 Eli Lilly's top products by revenue were Trulicity (USD 6,471.9m), Humalog (2,453.0m), COVID-19 antibodies (2,239.3m) and Taltz (2,212.8m); total revenue was USD 28,318.4m (U.S. 16,811.0m, outside U.S. 11,507.4m); Verzenio was 1,349.9m (+48%).

docs.t: CLM-001001 financials
docs.x: In FY2022 Trulicity was USD 7,439.7m, Verzenio 2,483.5m (+84%), Taltz 2,482.0m, Jardiance 2,066.0m, COVID-19 antibodies 2,023.5m (-10%), Alimta 927.7m (-55%); Mounjaro had its first revenue of USD 482.5m (U.S. 366.6m); total revenue USD 28,541.4m (U.S. 18,190.0m, outside U.S. 10,351.3m).

docs.t: CLM-001002 financials
docs.x: FY2023 revenue growth (USD 34,124.1m, +20%) was driven by Mounjaro, Verzenio and Jardiance and included one-time rights-sale revenue of USD 579.0m (Baqsimi, U.S.) and USD 1.45bn (olanzapine portfolio incl. Zyprexa, outside U.S.), while COVID-19 antibody revenue was zero versus USD 2,023.5m in 2022. Roughly USD 2.0bn of FY2023 revenue was non-recurring asset-sale revenue, so underlying 2023 growth was lower than the reported 20%.

docs.t: CLM-001003 financials
docs.x: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro + Zepbound) was 15.6% of Lilly revenue in FY2023 (USD 5,338.9m of 34,124.1m), 36.6% in FY2024 (USD 16,465.8m of 45,042.7m) and 56.0% in FY2025 (USD 36,507m of 65,179m); shares computed by the research team from 10-K disaggregated revenue tables. Revenue concentration in one molecule rose from ~16% to 56% in two years; Lilly itself flags this as a risk.

docs.t: CLM-001004 successes_failures
docs.x: Trulicity revenue was USD 6,471.9m (FY2021), 7,439.7m (FY2022), 7,132.6m (FY2023), 5,253.5m (FY2024) and 4,276m (FY2025); U.S. FY2025 2,914m vs 5,433m in FY2023. Internal cannibalisation: the prior GLP-1 franchise lost ~USD 3bn of annual revenue as tirzepatide replaced it.

docs.t: CLM-001005 financials
docs.x: Lilly's gross margin as a percent of revenue was 74.2% (FY2021), 76.8% (FY2022), 79.2% (FY2023), 81.3% (FY2024) and 83.0% (FY2025); the FY2025 10-K attributes the latest rise to favorable product mix and improved cost of production, partly offset by lower realized prices.

docs.t: CLM-001006 financials
docs.x: R&D expense excluding acquired IPR&D was 24.5% of revenue in FY2021, 25.2% in FY2022, 27.3% in FY2023, 24.4% in FY2024 and 20.5% in FY2025 (ratios computed from CLM-000133..147), while absolute R&D grew from USD 6.9bn to USD 13.3bn. Absolute R&D nearly doubled yet intensity fell, because revenue grew faster: operating leverage rather than under-investment.

docs.t: CLM-001007 financials
docs.x: Income before income taxes as a share of revenue was 21.7% (FY2021), 23.8% (FY2022), 19.2% (FY2023), 28.2% (FY2024) and 39.5% (FY2025), computed from CLM-000133-137 and CLM-000183-187.

docs.t: CLM-001008 financials
docs.x: Dividends paid and share repurchases were USD 3,086.8m / 1,250.0m (FY2021), 3,535.8m / 1,500.0m (FY2022), 4,069.3m / 750.0m (FY2023), 4,680.4m / 2,500.0m (FY2024) and 5,384m / 4,108m (FY2025). In FY2025 capital return (USD 9.5bn) was about 1.2x capex (USD 7.8bn): reinvestment is not crowding out distributions.

docs.t: CLM-001009 financials

docs.t: CLM-001010 successes_failures

docs.t: CLM-001011 successes_failures

docs.t: CLM-001055 tirzepatide pipeline
docs.x: ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT04184622 (SURMOUNT-1 Phase 3 obesity): Phase 3, lead sponsor Eli Lilly and Company, status COMPLETED, start 2019-12-04, enrollment 2539 (ACTUAL), primary completion 2022-04-01 (ACTUAL); official title: Efficacy and Safety of Tirzepatide Once Weekly in Participants Without Type 2 Diabetes Who Have Obesity or Are Overweight With Weight- Related Comorbidities: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial (SURMOUNT-1)

docs.t: CLM-001056 tirzepatide scientific_rd
docs.x: In the 72-week SURMOUNT-1 phase 3 trial (NCT04184622) tirzepatide reduced mean body weight by 15.0% (5 mg), 19.5% (10 mg) and 20.9% (15 mg) versus 3.1% with placebo in adults with obesity without diabetes (treatment-regimen estimand).

docs.t: CLM-001057 donanemab scientific_rd
docs.x: In the 76-week TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 phase 3 trial (1,736 participants, NCT04437511) donanemab slowed CDR-SB worsening by 0.67 points versus placebo in the low/medium tau population (P<.001); ARIA-E occurred in 24.0% (52 symptomatic) of donanemab patients versus 2.1% on placebo, and three treatment-related deaths occurred on donanemab versus one on placebo.

docs.t: CLM-001058 orforglipron scientific_rd
docs.x: In the 72-week ATTAIN-1 phase 3 trial (3,127 adults with obesity without diabetes, NCT05869903) once-daily oral orforglipron reduced mean body weight by 7.5% (6 mg), 8.4% (12 mg) and 11.2% (36 mg) versus 2.1% with placebo, with 5.3-10.3% treatment discontinuation due to adverse events versus 2.7% on placebo.

docs.t: CLM-001059 orforglipron scientific_rd
docs.x: In the 40-week ACHIEVE-1 phase 3 trial in early type 2 diabetes (559 participants) orforglipron lowered HbA1c by 1.24 to 1.48 percentage points across the 3 mg, 12 mg and 36 mg doses versus 0.41 with placebo.

docs.t: CLM-001060 retatrutide scientific_rd
docs.x: In the 80-week TRIUMPH-1 phase 3 trial (2,339 randomised adults with obesity without diabetes, NCT05929066) once-weekly retatrutide reduced mean body weight by 17.6% (4 mg), 23.7% (9 mg) and 25.0% (12 mg) versus 3.9% with placebo, published in NEJM on 5 November 2026. Retatrutide is the pipeline asset that could extend Lilly efficacy leadership beyond tirzepatide if approved and tolerated.

docs.t: CLM-001061 pipeline
docs.x: The FDA approved Jaypirca (pirtobrutinib; Lilly/Loxo) on 27 January 2023 for relapsed or refractory mantle cell lymphoma after at least two lines of therapy including a BTK inhibitor; the FY2022 10-K describes this as accelerated approval.

docs.t: CLM-001062 pipeline
docs.x: The FDA approved Omvoh (mirikizumab-mrkz; Lilly) on 26 October 2023 for ulcerative colitis, with Crohn's disease approved later in the U.S., EU and Japan per the FY2025 10-K.

docs.t: CLM-001063 pipeline
docs.x: The FDA approved Kisunla (donanemab-azbt; Lilly) on 2 July 2024 to treat Alzheimer's disease; the FY2025 10-K lists it as approved in the U.S., EU and Japan.

docs.t: CLM-001064 pipeline
docs.x: The FDA approved Ebglyss (lebrikizumab-lbkz; Lilly) on 13 September 2024 for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, after a 2023 complete response letter recorded in Lilly's FY2023 10-K.

docs.t: CLM-001065 pipeline
docs.x: The FDA approved Inluriyo (imlunestrant; Lilly) on 25 September 2025 for ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated advanced or metastatic breast cancer.

docs.t: CLM-001066 commercial_market_access
docs.x: The FDA removed tirzepatide from its drug shortage list on 2 October 2024 and, after a court-ordered reevaluation, confirmed on 19 December 2024 that the shortage was resolved, giving compounders a 60-90 day grace period; STAT reported the decision would stop companies making cheaper copies.

docs.t: CLM-001067 successes_failures
docs.x: On 10 June 2024 the FDA Peripheral and Central Nervous System Drugs Advisory Committee voted 11-0 that donanemab was effective and 11-0 that benefits outweighed risks for the mild cognitive impairment and mild dementia population studied, three weeks before FDA approval on 2 July 2024; FDA staff had raised concerns about exclusion of low-tau patients.

docs.t: CLM-001068 commercial_market_access
docs.x: On 1 March 2023 Lilly announced it would cut list prices of Humalog and Humulin by 70% (effective Q4 2023), set a $25 per vial non-branded insulin lispro, launch Rezvoglar at a 78% discount to Lantus, and cap out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 per month for commercially insured and uninsured patients; BioPharma Dive noted Humalog, Humulin and Basaglar sales had already fallen by double digits from 2021 to 2022. The insulin price cut gave up revenue in a shrinking franchise while building policy goodwill ahead of the 2025 pricing negotiation (INTERPRETATION by reporter and research team).

docs.t: CLM-001069 successes_failures
docs.x: Lilly's FY2025 10-K Note 16 lists ongoing litigation including its 2021 suit against HHS over 340B contract-pharmacy rules, a 340B antitrust class action (Second Circuit reversed dismissal), multidistrict insulin-pricing suits since 2017, Teva's Emgality patent appeal and the Brazil Cosmopolis facility labour case.

docs.t: CLM-003000 Humira business
docs.x: Humira lost U.S. exclusivity on January 31, 2023; AbbVie's FY2023 10-K states U.S. Humira sales fell 35% in 2023 and international sales 12% on direct biosimilar competition.

docs.t: CLM-003001 Humira financials
CLM-003002 Humira financials
docs.x: Global Humira net revenues were USD 20,694m (2021), 21,237m (2022), 14,404m (2023), 8,993m (2024) and 4,540m (2025); the 2025 figure is 21% of the 2022 peak.

docs.t: CLM-003003 Humira financials
docs.x: International Humira net revenues were USD 3,364m (2021), 2,618m (2022), 2,244m (2023), 1,851m (2024) and 1,478m (2025); international sales were already falling in 2022, a year before U.S. entry, after the EU patent expired in most countries in October 2018.

docs.t: CLM-003004 Humira financials
docs.x: Humira was about 37% of AbbVie net revenues in 2021 and 2022 (43% in 2020), about 27% in 2023, and, by the analyst's computation from reported figures, about 16% in 2024 and 7% in 2025.

docs.t: CLM-003005 Humira competitive_advantage
docs.x: AbbVie's FY2021 10-K states the U.S. composition-of-matter patent for Humira expired in December 2016 and the equivalent EU patent expired in most EU countries in October 2018; U.S. biosimilar sales nevertheless began only on January 31, 2023. The 6+ year gap between composition-of-matter expiry and U.S. entry is consistent with secondary patents and settlements doing the exclusivity work; AJMC (metadata only) says biosimilar settlements deferred entry to 2023.

docs.t: CLM-003006 Humira commercial_market_access
docs.x: Amgen launched Amjevita, the first U.S. Humira biosimilar, on January 31, 2023 at list prices 55% and 5% below Humira's; eight more adalimumab biosimilars followed in 2023 (seven in July and Pfizer's Abrilada in November), for nine in the year.

docs.t: CLM-003007 Humira commercial_market_access
docs.x: IQVIA claims data show Humira kept at least 97% of total U.S. adalimumab volume through March 2024, 14 months after biosimilar entry, because rebate-for-access contracting left payers little incentive to switch. Volume retention, not just price, explains why Humira US revenue fell 35% in 2023 rather than collapsing; net-price erosion (rebates) carried most of the 2023 decline.

docs.t: CLM-003008 Humira commercial_market_access
docs.x: CVS Caremark announced on January 3, 2024 that from April 1, 2024 it would remove Humira from its major national commercial template formularies and cover biosimilars, while AbbVie agreed to supply Cordavis (a CVS Health company) with a committed volume of co-branded Humira.

docs.t: CLM-003009 Humira commercial_market_access
docs.x: Hyrimoz (Sandoz, co-promoted with Cordavis) rose from 1% to 14% of U.S. adalimumab claims in April 2024 and 16% in June 2024, and a Cordavis-labelled Humira reached 5% of claims by June 2024.

docs.t: CLM-003010 Humira financials
docs.x: U.S. Humira net revenues fell 41% in 2024 and 57% in 2025, after falling 35% in 2023, so the steepest declines followed the April 2024 PBM formulary change. Association in time, not proven causation: PBM exclusion, biosimilar maturity and Medicare Part D dynamics all moved together.

docs.t: CLM-003011 Humira policy_regulation
docs.x: Two putative class actions over Humira pricing are disclosed in the FY2025 10-K: Camargo v. AbbVie (filed April 2023, N.D. Ill.) and Sheet Metal Workers' Health Plan v. AbbVie (filed January 2025, N.D. Ill.); allegations are unproven.

docs.t: CLM-003012 Skyrizi financials
CLM-003013 Rinvoq financials
CLM-003014 financials
docs.x: Skyrizi plus Rinvoq revenue rose from USD 7,687m in 2022 to 25,866m in 2025 (+18,179m) while Humira fell from 21,237m to 4,540m (-16,697m), so the two successors more than replaced the lost Humira revenue by 2025. Total company revenue passed its 2022 peak (USD 58,054m) only in 2025 (61,160m), i.e. the replacement took three years.

docs.t: CLM-003015 financials
docs.x: AbbVie total net revenues were USD 58,054m in 2022 (+3.3%), 54,318m in 2023 (-6.4%), 56,334m in 2024 (+3.7%) and 61,160m in 2025 (+8.6%); U.S. revenue fell 8.4% in 2023.

docs.t: CLM-003016 Skyrizi Rinvoq pipeline
docs.x: Skyrizi gained U.S. approvals for psoriatic arthritis (January 2022), Crohn's disease (June 2022) and ulcerative colitis (June 2024); Rinvoq gained atopic dermatitis (January 2022), ulcerative colitis (March 2022), Crohn's disease (May 2023) and giant cell arteritis (April 2025). Together these indications cover Humira's gastroenterology, dermatology and rheumatology uses, which is the mechanism by which switching stayed inside AbbVie.

docs.t: CLM-003017 Rinvoq policy_regulation
docs.x: On September 1, 2021 FDA required boxed-warning updates for JAK inhibitors including Rinvoq (serious heart events, cancer, blood clots, death) on the basis of the Xeljanz ORAL Surveillance trial; AbbVie's December 3, 2021 release said the U.S. Rinvoq label added mortality, MACE, malignancy and thrombosis warnings and limited the RA indication to patients with inadequate response or intolerance to one or more TNF blockers. The JAK class warning is a standing label risk to Rinvoq's first-line use; AbbVie's October 2025 sNDA allowing use before TNF blockers in UC/Crohn's (10-K) suggests FDA has accepted some pre-TNF positioning.

docs.t: CLM-003018 Rinvoq pipeline
docs.x: In October 2025 FDA approved an sNDA allowing Rinvoq in ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease before TNF blockers in patients for whom TNF blockers are clinically inadvisable and who received at least one approved systemic therapy; in October 2025 AbbVie also reported positive Phase 3b/4 SELECT-SWITCH data in which Rinvoq beat Humira in RA after one prior TNF inhibitor.

docs.t: CLM-003019 Rinvoq pipeline
docs.x: Rinvoq has positive Phase 3 toplines in alopecia areata (UP-AA studies 1 and 2, July-August 2025) and non-segmental vitiligo (October 2025); an EMA application for alopecia areata was filed in November 2025 and U.S./EU vitiligo applications in February 2026.

docs.t: CLM-003020 Skyrizi pipeline
docs.x: In 2026 FDA approved subcutaneous induction of Skyrizi in Crohn's disease (supported by the Phase 3 AFFIRM study) and updated the label so clinicians may use judgment on tuberculosis testing across all indications.

docs.t: CLM-003021 Skyrizi Rinvoq competitive_advantage
docs.x: AbbVie's FY2025 10-K states U.S. composition-of-matter patents for risankizumab (Skyrizi) and upadacitinib (Rinvoq) expire in 2033; after September 2025 settlements with all generic filers, no generic Rinvoq tablet entry is expected before April 2037 in the U.S. if pediatric exclusivity is granted. Rinvoq's practical exclusivity runs 4 years past its composition patent. Skyrizi, a biologic, still faces biosimilar risk after 2033 and no settlement-based date is disclosed.

docs.t: CLM-003022 financials
docs.x: AbbVie raised its 2027 Skyrizi plus Rinvoq sales target to USD 27bn in February 2024 and to more than USD 31bn (Skyrizi about 20bn, Rinvoq about 11bn per Fierce) in early 2025; Reuters (April 2026) restates the more-than-31bn figure. With 2025 actual at 25.9bn and nine-month 2026 at 23.1bn, the 31bn mark looks reachable in 2026, a year early (analyst arithmetic).

docs.t: CLM-003023 Skyrizi Rinvoq Humira financials
docs.x: For the nine months to September 30, 2026 AbbVie reported Skyrizi USD 15,764m, Rinvoq 7,350m and Humira 2,127m (Humira -35.4% reported); Q3 2026 net revenues were USD 17,404m (+10.3%).

docs.t: CLM-003024 financials
docs.x: Reuters reported Q1 2026 Humira global sales of USD 688m (-38.6%), Skyrizi USD 4.48bn (+30.9%) and Rinvoq USD 2.12bn (+23.3%).

docs.t: CLM-003025 Imbruvica financials
docs.x: Imbruvica global net revenues fell from USD 5,408m (2021) to 4,568m (2022), 3,596m (2023), 3,347m (2024) and 2,869m (2025); U.S. product revenue was 4,321m in 2021 and 2,048m in 2025.

docs.t: CLM-003026 Imbruvica policy_regulation
docs.x: CMS selected Imbruvica among the first 10 Medicare Part D drugs for price negotiation (initial price applicability year 2026); AbbVie recorded a USD 2.1bn pre-tax impairment of the U.S. Imbruvica intangible in Q3 2023 (fair value USD 1.9bn versus USD 4.0bn carrying value, as of August 29, 2023).

docs.t: CLM-003027 Venclexta successes_failures
docs.x: Venclexta net revenues were USD 1,820m (2021), 2,009m (2022), 2,288m (2023), 2,583m (2024) and 2,792m (2025); the Phase 3 CANOVA study in myeloma (September 2023) and the Phase 3 VERONA study in higher-risk MDS (June 2025, overall survival) did not meet their primary endpoints.

docs.t: CLM-003028 Vraylar financials
docs.x: Vraylar net revenues were USD 1,728m (2021), 2,038m (2022), 2,759m (2023), 3,267m (2024) and 3,621m (2025); CMS selected Vraylar for Medicare price-setting effective 2027 (selection January 2025).

docs.t: CLM-003029 Vraylar competitive_advantage
docs.x: Guggenheim (via BioSpace, November 2024) put Vraylar's next patent expiry in September 2029. Vraylar (3.6bn, 2025) is the next large LOE and also an IRA-negotiation product from 2027.

docs.t: CLM-003030 Botox Therapeutic financials
docs.x: Botox Therapeutic net revenues were USD 2,451m (2021), 2,719m (2022), 2,991m (2023), 3,283m (2024) and 3,769m (2025); CMS selected Botox for Medicare price-setting in January 2026.

docs.t: CLM-003031 Botox Cosmetic Juvederm financials
docs.x: Botox Cosmetic net revenues were USD 2,232m (2021), 2,615m (2022), 2,682m (2023), 2,720m (2024) and 2,602m (2025); Juvederm fell from 1,535m (2021) to 993m (2025).

docs.t: CLM-003032 Botox Cosmetic Juvederm successes_failures
docs.x: AbbVie attributes the 11% 2025 decline in U.S. Botox Cosmetic revenue to unfavorable pricing from customer loyalty program changes, lower market share and decreased consumer demand; Juvederm fell 15% on lower consumer demand.

docs.t: CLM-003033 Botox Cosmetic successes_failures
docs.x: AbbVie launched a revised Allē loyalty program in October 2024, reinstated the original program in early 2025 after providers found the new one too complex, and said aesthetics would see a one-time price adjustment in Q1 2025; aesthetics Q4 2024 sales fell 4.4% to USD 1.3bn. A consumer-facing loyalty mechanism that is central to the Botox franchise's provider stickiness was changed without sufficient provider testing; the reversal within months shows it was reversible but cost revenue.

docs.t: CLM-003034 Botox Cosmetic Juvederm successes_failures
docs.x: At Q4 2024 AbbVie's CFO lowered the 2029 aesthetics expectation from USD 9bn to 'somewhere north of $7 billion'; analysts cited by BioSpace put 2029 sales near USD 7.0-7.6bn.

docs.t: CLM-003035 CoolSculpting Liletta Resonic Durysta successes_failures
docs.x: AbbVie recorded USD 1.4bn of intangible impairment in Q4 2023 after cutting sales and marketing for CoolSculpting (fair value 290m vs 1.3bn carrying) and Liletta, and in Q3 2025 discontinued the Resonic cellulite device (407m full impairment) and cut investment in Durysta (partial impairment); the 2025 charge was USD 847m.

docs.t: CLM-003036 Elahere financials
docs.x: Elahere U.S. net revenues were USD 477m in 2024 (first year after the ImmunoGen close) and 607m in 2025 (+27.2%); global Elahere revenue grew 43% in 2025 partly on a full year of ownership.

docs.t: CLM-003037 Ubrelvy Qulipta Vyalev financials
docs.x: Ubrelvy grew from USD 552m (2021) to 1,271m (2025), Qulipta from zero to 1,036m (first sales 2022), and Vyalev reached USD 482m in 2025 (U.S. 167m, international 315m) from 99m in 2024.

docs.t: CLM-003038 financials
docs.x: GAAP gross margin was 62% in 2023, 70% in 2024 and 70% in 2025; GAAP R&D (including intangible impairments) was 14% of revenue in 2023, 23% in 2024 and 15% in 2025; SG&A was 24%, 26% and 23%.

docs.t: CLM-003039 financials
docs.x: By the analyst's arithmetic on audited figures, GAAP operating margin was 31.9% in 2021, 31.2% in 2022, 23.5% in 2023, 16.2% in 2024 and 24.6% in 2025.

docs.t: CLM-003040 financials
docs.x: Intangible amortization was USD 7.9bn (2023), 7.6bn (2024) and 7.4bn (2025), with scheduled expense of 6.7bn (2026), 6.1bn (2027), 6.2bn (2028), 5.7bn (2029) and 4.5bn (2030); the 2025 change in fair value of contingent consideration was a USD 6.5bn charge (3.8bn in 2024). GAAP net income of 4.2bn in 2025 on 15.1bn operating income is largely non-cash and acquisition-driven: amortization (7.4bn) and the contingent-consideration charge (6.5bn) together total 13.9bn, 3.3 times GAAP net income of 4.2bn.

docs.t: CLM-003041 financials
docs.x: AbbVie's 10-K contingent consideration liabilities fair-value change was USD 6,495m in 2025, 3,771m in 2024 and 5,128m in 2023, and payments of contingent consideration were 2,865m, 1,995m and 870m (financing section of the cash flow statement). The FY2021 10-K ties USD 2.7bn of 2021 contingent-consideration expense to Skyrizi (Boehringer Ingelheim milestones); the 2025 10-K does not attribute the 6.5bn by product in the text read.

docs.t: CLM-003042 financials
docs.x: AbbVie's non-current long-term debt fell from USD 75,962m (2021) to 63,128m (2022) and 59,245m (2023), then rose to 66,841m (2024) after USD 15.0bn of notes financed ImmunoGen and Cerevel, and was 64,503m at end-2025.

docs.t: CLM-003043 financials
docs.x: Cash dividends paid were USD 10,539m (2023), 11,025m (2024) and 11,657m (2025); declared dividends per share were USD 5.99, 6.29 and 6.65; the quarterly dividend rose from USD 1.64 to 1.73 (declared October 2025) and to 1.82 (announced October 30, 2026).

docs.t: CLM-003044 financials
docs.x: AbbVie repurchased 7 million shares for USD 1.3bn in 2024 and 3 million for USD 606m in 2025, leaving USD 2.9bn of authorization at December 31, 2025.

docs.t: CLM-003045 partnerships_ma
docs.x: Acquired IPR&D and milestones upfront charges were USD 582m (2023), 2,627m (2024) and 4,808m (2025) in the FY2025 10-K table.

docs.t: CLM-003046 business
docs.x: AbbVie states Skyrizi, Humira and Rinvoq each exceeded 10% of net revenues and together were about 47% of 2024 revenue; three wholesalers (McKesson, Cardinal, Cencora) account for substantially all U.S. pharmaceutical sales.

docs.t: CLM-003047 pipeline
docs.x: AbbVie describes about 90 compounds, devices or indications in development, about 60 of them in mid- and late-stage development, across immunology, neuroscience, oncology, aesthetics and obesity.

docs.t: CLM-003048 partnerships_ma
docs.x: AbbVie completed the Allergan acquisition on May 8, 2020 in a cash and stock transaction that issued 286 million AbbVie shares at USD 83.96.

docs.t: CLM-003049 partnerships_ma
docs.x: AbbVie expected about USD 2.5bn of annual cost synergies from Allergan in 2022 (FY2021 10-K) and reported that it realized USD 2.5bn of annual cost synergies in 2022 (FY2022 10-K). Cost synergies were delivered on schedule; revenue synergies are less evident in the aesthetics franchise after 2023.

docs.t: CLM-003050 partnerships_ma
docs.x: BioSpace describes Allergan as a USD 63bn acquisition that gave AbbVie its aesthetics franchise; BioSpace also reports company-stated U.S. toxin share of about 60% for Botox and 40% for Juvederm in fillers at Q4 2024.

docs.t: CLM-003051 successes_failures
docs.x: In 2019 AbbVie terminated the Rova-T program (Stemcentrx acquisition, 2016) and impaired the remaining USD 1.0bn of IPR&D.

docs.t: CLM-003052 emraclidine tavapadon partnerships_ma
docs.x: AbbVie announced on December 6, 2023 the acquisition of Cerevel Therapeutics for USD 45.00 per share in cash (about USD 8.7bn equity value) and closed it on August 1, 2024; the announcement called emraclidine a potential best-in-class antipsychotic.

docs.t: CLM-003053 Elahere partnerships_ma
docs.x: AbbVie announced on November 30, 2023 the acquisition of ImmunoGen for USD 31.26 per share (about USD 10.1bn) and completed it on February 12, 2024; consideration transferred was USD 9.8bn (9.2bn net of cash acquired).

docs.t: CLM-003054 emraclidine successes_failures
docs.x: On November 11, 2024 AbbVie announced that both Phase 2 EMPOWER trials of emraclidine in acute schizophrenia missed the primary PANSS endpoint at week 6; AbbVie shares fell 12% at the open that day.

docs.t: CLM-003055 emraclidine pipeline
docs.x: The two emraclidine Phase 2 registry records show 385 participants (NCT05227690, 10 and 30 mg) and 391 participants (NCT05227703, 15 and 30 mg), both completed with primary completion in August 2024; a 698-participant extension study (NCT05443724) has status TERMINATED with primary completion June 25, 2025.

docs.t: CLM-003056 emraclidine successes_failures
docs.x: Stifel analysts said the placebo response in both EMPOWER trials was very high, while BMO urged investors not to blame placebo; BMO also credited AbbVie with 'expertly managing' the Humira loss of exclusivity. A high placebo response is a known failure mode in schizophrenia trials, but it is also a design risk the Phase 1b-to-Phase 2 jump should have priced in.

docs.t: CLM-003057 emraclidine successes_failures
docs.x: AbbVie recorded a USD 4.5bn pre-tax impairment of the emraclidine IPR&D in Q4 2024 (fair value USD 2.4bn versus USD 6.9bn carrying value as of November 11, 2024), charged to R&D; operating losses attributable to Cerevel through December 31, 2024 were USD 4.9bn.

docs.t: CLM-003058 emraclidine successes_failures
docs.x: TESTED PREMISE: that the emraclidine-related impairment was about USD 3.5bn and recognized in 2025. The audited filings show USD 4.5bn recognized in Q4 2024; the 2025 intangible impairment was USD 847m and related to Resonic and Durysta, not emraclidine.

docs.t: CLM-003059 financials
docs.x: Intangible asset impairment charges in the cash-flow statement were USD 4,229m (2023), 4,476m (2024) and 847m (2025).

docs.t: CLM-003060 successes_failures
docs.x: In Q1 2023 AbbVie impaired USD 630m of IPR&D for AGN-151607 (a neurotoxin for postoperative atrial fibrillation) after revising its R&D plan.

docs.t: CLM-003061 Vyalev successes_failures
docs.x: FDA issued a Complete Response Letter for ABBV-951 (foscarbidopa/foslevodopa) in March 2023 asking for more device (pump) information, AbbVie resubmitted in December 2023, FDA issued a second CRL in June 2024 citing observations at a third-party manufacturer without safety, efficacy or labeling issues, and approved Vyalev on October 17, 2024.

docs.t: CLM-003062 Vyalev pipeline
docs.x: The Vyalev approval rested on a 12-week Phase 3 versus oral immediate-release carbidopa/levodopa and a 52-week open-label safety study, and AbbVie said Medicare coverage was expected in the second half of 2025; EU launch (as Produodopa) was in January 2024.

docs.t: CLM-003063 tavapadon pipeline
docs.x: Tavapadon reported positive Phase 3 toplines in early Parkinson's disease (TEMPO-1, September 2024; TEMPO-2, December 2024), AbbVie submitted the NDA in September 2025, and AbbVie announced FDA approval of Juvmo (tavapadon) on September 28, 2026.

docs.t: CLM-003064 tavapadon pipeline
docs.x: ClinicalTrials.gov lists three completed tavapadon Phase 3 trials (NCT04201093 fixed-dose, 529 participants; NCT04223193 flexible-dose, 304; NCT04542499 TEMPO-3 adjunctive, 507) and an open-label Phase 3 (NCT04760769, 992 participants).

docs.t: CLM-003065 tavapadon partnerships_ma
docs.x: Cerevel's tavapadon was funded by arrangements AbbVie assumed (financing liability USD 246m at acquisition) that require repayment of regulatory and sales milestones and royalties on FDA approval, and AbbVie may owe Pfizer up to USD 1.6bn in milestones under a licence assumed from Cerevel.

docs.t: CLM-003066 Emrelis pipeline
docs.x: FDA granted accelerated approval to Emrelis (telisotuzumab vedotin) on May 14, 2025 for previously treated non-squamous NSCLC with high c-Met overexpression, on an overall response rate of 35% (n=84) and median response duration of 7.2 months from the single-arm LUMINOSITY study, with a companion diagnostic.

docs.t: CLM-003067 Epkinly pivekimab sunirine TrenibotE pipeline
docs.x: AbbVie reported in 2025: Epkinly plus rituximab and lenalidomide approved for relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (November 2025); Epkinly Phase 3 in relapsed/refractory DLBCL improved PFS but not overall survival (January 2026); a BLA for pivekimab sunirine in BPDCN submitted (September 2025); and a BLA for TrenibotE in glabellar lines submitted (April 2025).

docs.t: CLM-003068 ABBV-400 pipeline
docs.x: ClinicalTrials.gov lists telisotuzumab adizutecan (ABBV-400) trials including a Phase 2 started November 2024 (NCT06614192) and a Phase 3 with a start date of May 22, 2026 (NCT07525206); AbbVie's FY2024 10-K reports a Phase 3 in c-Met-overexpressed refractory colorectal cancer starting December 2024.

docs.t: CLM-003069 lutikizumab pipeline
docs.x: AbbVie reported positive Phase 3 INTREPID topline for lutikizumab in hidradenitis suppurativa (met HiSCR 75 at week 16) and plans regulatory submissions in the second half of 2027; a Phase 3 record (NCT06468228) shows primary completion December 2026.

docs.t: CLM-003070 ABBV-466 zumilokibart pipeline
docs.x: At UEG Week 2026 AbbVie presented Phase 2a TARGET-CD data for ABBV-466 (Skyrizi plus ABBV-382) showing higher endoscopic remission than either component alone at week 12 in Crohn's disease, and in 2026 completed the acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics (zumilokibart, an IL-13 antibody in atopic dermatitis, and APG273).

docs.t: CLM-003071 pivekimab sunirine pipeline
docs.x: ClinicalTrials.gov lists a Phase 2/3 pivekimab sunirine study (NCT07581002) starting June 2026 with primary completion in 2032.

docs.t: CLM-003072 CPTX2309 partnerships_ma
docs.x: AbbVie agreed on June 30, 2025 to acquire Capstan Therapeutics (CPTX2309, a Phase 1 in vivo anti-CD19 CAR-T delivered by targeted lipid nanoparticles for B-cell autoimmune disease) for up to USD 2.1bn cash, and the FY2025 10-K records a USD 1.9bn acquired IPR&D upfront charge for Capstan; closing was announced August 19, 2025.

docs.t: CLM-003073 GUB014295 partnerships_ma
docs.x: AbbVie licensed Gubra's amylin analog GUB014295 (Phase 1, NCT06144684) on March 3, 2025 for USD 350m upfront and up to USD 1.875bn in milestones, calling it AbbVie's entry into obesity; FY2025 10-K lists obesity among 2026 growth areas.

docs.t: CLM-003074 partnerships_ma
docs.x: Per the FY2025 10-K and canonical claims, AbbVie also closed Nimble Therapeutics (January 23, 2025), recorded a USD 906m upfront charge for Gilgamesh and USD 700m for an Ichnos Glenmark licence in 2025; Aliada (2024), Landos and Celsius were not researched in this shard.

docs.t: CLM-003075 partnerships_ma
docs.x: AbbVie's FY2025 10-K lists 'maximizing the value of key acquisitions as well as continuing to invest in external innovation' among its strategy pillars, and its acquired IPR&D charges rose from USD 582m (2023) to 4,808m (2025).

docs.t: CLM-003076 leadership
docs.x: AbbVie announced on February 20, 2024 that Robert A. Michael (president and COO) would succeed Richard A. Gonzalez as CEO on July 1, 2024 with Gonzalez becoming executive chairman; the board then elected Michael chairman effective July 1, 2025 when Gonzalez retired from the board.

docs.t: CLM-003077 leadership
docs.x: Michael's AbbVie roles were CFO (2019-2021, then vice chairman for finance and commercial operations to June 2022), vice chairman and president (June 2022-July 2023), president and COO (July 2023-June 2024) and CEO (July 2024); Gonzalez's release credited him with navigating the Humira exclusivity end and the Allergan, ImmunoGen and Cerevel deals.

docs.t: CLM-003078 leadership
docs.x: As of the FY2025 10-K the executive officers include Michael (chairman and CEO), Scott T. Reents (CFO, an officer since June 2022; previously tax and treasury), Jeffrey R. Stewart (chief commercial officer, at AbbVie/Abbott since 1992), Roopal Thakkar (EVP R&D and chief scientific officer), Nicholas Donoghoe (chief business and strategy officer) and Azita Saleki-Gerhardt (chief operations officer).

docs.t: CLM-003079 leadership
docs.x: Every executive named in the FY2025 10-K officer list with a disclosed biography has prior Abbott or AbbVie roles in finance, commercial, operations or R&D; the CEO transition was internal and planned 'for some time' per the board. Continuity reduced execution risk through the Humira transition but also concentrates the deal-making judgement that produced the emraclidine miss in the same team.

docs.t: CLM-003080 policy_regulation
docs.x: Under the Inflation Reduction Act CMS selected Imbruvica (2023, prices from 2026), Vraylar and Linzess (January 2025, prices from 2027), and Botox (January 2026) for Medicare Part D/B price setting.

docs.t: CLM-003081 policy_regulation
docs.x: In January 2026 AbbVie announced an agreement with the U.S. government to offer low Medicaid prices and direct-to-patient offerings (including Humira through TrumpRx) and pledged USD 100bn of U.S. R&D and capital investment over a decade, in exchange for a three-year exemption from tariffs and future price mandates.

docs.t: CLM-003082 policy_regulation
docs.x: TESTED PREMISE: that AbbVie made a USD 10bn U.S. manufacturing pledge in 2025. No such pledge was located; the filings read show construction starts in Illinois (API facility) and Massachusetts (biologics) in 2025 and a January 2026 agreement to buy an Arizona device plant, within a USD 100bn ten-year pledge announced January 2026.

docs.t: CLM-003083 data_ai
docs.x: AbbVie announced a Valkai life-sciences AI partnership for clinical development on September 29, 2026 (canonical CLM-000285); no outcome metrics were found in this shard's sources.

docs.t: CLM-003084 competitive_advantage
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: AbbVie's Humira replacement worked because the successor assets were already launched, were expanded to Humira's major indications before U.S. exclusivity ended, and carried head-to-head evidence, so prescriber and payer switching stayed in-house. Replication path: launch the next-generation molecule in the same prescriber call point 3-5 years before the cliff and fund indication breadth and head-to-head data.

docs.t: CLM-003085 commercial_market_access
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: AbbVie delayed U.S. Humira erosion by rebate-for-access contracting that kept at least 97% of adalimumab volume through March 2024, and then adapted to the CVS Caremark/Cordavis exclusion by supplying a co-branded Humira, which captured 23% of Humira-switchers in 2024 versus 60% for co-promoted Hyrimoz. The defence bought roughly a year of volume; the lesson is that PBM vertical integration (Cordavis, Quallent) changes the contracting game faster than patent strategy.

docs.t: CLM-003086 competitive_advantage
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: AbbVie's business-development model buys late-stage or commercial assets to refill the pipeline and accepts binary failure risk; 2024's USD 18.5bn of cash paid for ImmunoGen and Cerevel produced one large write-down (emraclidine, 4.5bn), one growing product (Elahere, 607m U.S. in 2025) and one approved drug (Juvmo, 2026). BD&L is a repeatable capability but its hit rate on first-in-class psychiatry assets was poor; the evidence does not yet show positive returns on the 2024 deals.

docs.t: CLM-003087 competitive_advantage
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: AbbVie's settlement-based IP strategy converts patent expiry dates into negotiated entry dates: Humira biosimilar entry was negotiated to 2023 and Rinvoq generic entry is not expected before April 2037, four years after its 2033 composition-of-matter patents. Rinvoq exclusivity beyond 2033 is a strategic asset with a verified source; Humira settlement history needs the court and SEC filings.

docs.t: CLM-003088 competitive_advantage
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: AbbVie's aesthetics franchise depends on consumer demand and a provider loyalty mechanism (Allē, provider programs); the 2024 loyalty redesign reduced share and pricing, showing the franchise is exposed to discretionary-spending cycles and to its own channel design.

docs.t: CLM-003089 pipeline
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: post-2030 growth depends on five groups: Skyrizi/Rinvoq lifecycle (patents to 2033/2037), neuroscience launches (Vyalev, Juvmo, Vraylar's decline from 2029), oncology ADCs (Elahere, Emrelis, ABBV-400), obesity and in vivo CAR-T options (Gubra, Capstan, Phase 1), and a rebuilt aesthetics line; the pipeline is broad but its late-stage assets outside immunology are mostly small or unproven.

docs.t: CLM-003090 strategy
docs.x: RECOMMENDATION (for the Takeda comparison): treat AbbVie's Humira response as a three-part template - pre-built successors, a contracting defence that buys time, and diversification through acquisitions sized to survive a write-down - and treat its neuroscience BD as high-variance.

docs.t: CLM-005000 financials
docs.x: Takeda revenue (IFRS, fiscal years ending 31 March) was JPY 3,569.0bn (FY2021), 4,027.5bn (FY2022), 4,263.8bn (FY2023), 4,581.6bn (FY2024) and 4,505.7bn (FY2025, year to 31 March 2026). Revenue is roughly flat-to-down in the latest year at actual FX after a 2021-2024 rise; the FY2025 decline is driven by VYVANSE erosion (see loe claims).

docs.t: CLM-005001 financials
docs.x: FY2025 revenue declined 1.7% at actual exchange rates and 2.7% at constant exchange rates; U.S. revenue fell 9.0% AER (-7.7% CER) to JPY 2,164.8bn, while Europe and Canada rose 8.6% AER (+3.0% CER) to JPY 1,146.2bn. Takeda's reported growth depends materially on JPY/USD; CER shows an underlying decline in FY2025.

docs.t: CLM-005002 financials
docs.x: The United States accounted for JPY 2,164.8bn of JPY 4,505.7bn FY2025 revenue (about 48%); Japan JPY 433.1bn (about 10%); China JPY 195.1bn (about 4%); in FY2024 the U.S. was JPY 2,379.7bn of 4,581.6bn (about 52%). Takeda is U.S.-concentrated and therefore exposed to U.S. pricing policy and the dollar; Japan is a small share of revenue despite being the domicile.

docs.t: CLM-005003 financials
docs.x: Takeda Core Operating Profit (company-defined non-IFRS) was JPY 955.2bn (FY2021, implied), 1,188.4bn (FY2022), 1,054.9bn (FY2023), 1,162.6bn (FY2024) and 1,172.5bn (FY2025). FY2021 is derived as FY2022 minus the reported +233.2bn change. Core profit has been broadly stable around JPY 1.05-1.19 trillion despite the Vyvanse cliff, helped by cost programs and FX.

docs.t: CLM-005004 financials
docs.x: Takeda R&D expense was JPY 526.1bn (FY2021), 633.3bn (FY2022), 729.9bn (FY2023), 730.2bn (FY2024) and 675.9bn (FY2025); the FY2025 decrease was attributed to lower expenses as development programs were terminated or progressed and to mezagitamab co-development funding. R&D fell 7.4% in FY2025 even as the late-stage pipeline filed; the savings partly reflect portfolio pruning rather than a retrenchment of late-stage funding (interpretation).

docs.t: CLM-005005 financials
docs.x: Takeda's adjusted net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio was 2.6x at 31 March 2023, 3.1x at 31 March 2024, 2.8x at 31 March 2025 and 2.6x at 31 March 2026 (adjusted net debt JPY 3,817.6bn, adjusted EBITDA JPY 1,457.2bn at March 2026). Deleveraging from the Shire acquisition has largely been achieved; leverage briefly rose in FY2023 and is back to 2.6x, leaving limited but non-zero capacity for large M&A (interpretation).

docs.t: CLM-005006 financials
docs.x: Takeda follows a progressive dividend policy (increase or maintain annual dividend per share, with buybacks when appropriate); dividends were JPY 200 per share for FY2025 and are intended at JPY 204 per share for the year ending March 2027; cash dividends paid were JPY 288.5bn, 303.9bn and 313.2bn in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025. Dividends of about JPY 313bn per year are a fixed claim on cash flow while the company funds launches and restructuring.

docs.t: CLM-005007 financials
docs.x: Capital expenditures (PP&E and intangible assets) were JPY 496.7bn (FY2023), 319.4bn (FY2024) and 426.9bn (FY2025); the FY2025 filing cites plasma manufacturing capacity expansion among ongoing projects.

docs.t: CLM-005008 financials
docs.x: Growth & Launch Products accounted for JPY 1,833.0bn (43% of revenue) in FY2023, JPY 2,201.9bn (48%) in FY2024 and JPY 2,313.3bn (51%) in FY2025; Takeda retires the Growth & Launch category from FY2026 in favour of 'New Launches' and 'Core In-Line Brands'. Category definitions change annually; comparisons across years use Takeda's then-current product lists.

docs.t: CLM-005009 financials
docs.x: FY2025 revenue by product: ENTYVIO JPY 958.0bn (21% of revenue), immunoglobulin brands JPY 790.6bn (18%), TAKHZYRO JPY 223.9bn (5%), VYVANSE/ELVANSE JPY 203.2bn, GATTEX/REVESTIVE JPY 145.7bn, ALBUMIN JPY 140.3bn (3%), TRINTELLIX JPY 121.8bn, FRUZAQLA JPY 55.1bn, LIVTENCITY JPY 46.9bn, QDENGA JPY 40.8bn, ADZYNMA JPY 12.0bn, EOHILIA JPY 8.8bn. Two franchises (Entyvio and plasma immunoglobulins) are 39% of revenue; the next product is below 5%.

docs.t: CLM-005010 business
docs.x: Takeda's six key business areas (GI, Rare Diseases, PDT, Oncology, Vaccines, Neuroscience) accounted for 95.0% of FY2025 revenue; the company had about 47,029 employees at 31 March 2026 (47,455 in 2025; 49,281 in 2024).

docs.t: CLM-005011 financials
docs.x: In the six months to 30 September 2026 (H1 FY2026) revenue was JPY 2,407.0bn (+8.4% AER, -1.0% CER), operating profit JPY 406.7bn (+60.4%), and Takeda forecast FY2026 revenue of JPY 4,700bn and Core Operating Profit of JPY 1,190bn (+1.5%) including restructuring expenses of JPY 160bn. Underlying (CER) revenue is still declining in the first half of FY2026 while the launch wave has not yet started to contribute.

docs.t: CLM-005012 financials
docs.x: H1 FY2026 U.S. revenue was JPY 1,130.7bn (+3.6% AER, -5.4% CER) and ENTYVIO sales were JPY 541.7bn (+13.0% AER, +2.7% CER), with U.S. ENTYVIO at JPY 351.8bn driven by FX and subcutaneous growth. At constant currency, Entyvio grows only about 3%, which matters for the 2030-32 exclusivity window.

docs.t: CLM-005013 successes_failures
docs.x: On 18 May 2026 a U.S. federal jury (D. Mass.) awarded plaintiffs USD 884,943,990 in single damages against Takeda in the AMITIZA pay-for-delay antitrust litigation; wholesaler-class and retailer damages are to be trebled on entry of judgment; Takeda says it will pursue post-trial motions and appeal. Legal exposure (before trebling) exceeds USD 0.88bn and may require cash outflows after appeal; trebling could multiply the wholesaler/retailer components.

docs.t: CLM-005014 financials
docs.x: Takeda recognised a JPY 403.5bn provision for legal proceedings in FY2025 following the AMITIZA verdict, which pushed reported operating profit to JPY 6.2bn and net loss to JPY 152.1bn in FY2025; Core Operating Profit was unaffected at JPY 1,172.5bn. Reported and core profit tell different stories in FY2025; analysis should state which basis is used.

docs.t: CLM-005015 successes_failures
docs.x: VYVANSE/ELVANSE revenue fell from JPY 423.2bn (FY2023) to JPY 350.6bn (FY2024) and JPY 203.2bn (FY2025, -42% AER); its U.S. composition-of-matter patent and pediatric exclusivity expired in August 2023 and Takeda expects the decline to continue in FY2026. The Vyvanse cliff removed roughly JPY 220bn of annual revenue in two years and is the main reason reported revenue is not growing.

docs.t: CLM-005016 successes_failures
docs.x: AZILVA revenue fell from JPY 33.6bn (FY2023) to JPY 11.8bn and JPY 7.1bn (FY2025) after a generic approval in Japan in February 2023; TRINTELLIX (JPY 121.8bn in FY2025) is expected to face generic competition after certain patent rights expire in December 2026. Trintellix loss of exclusivity falls inside FY2026 (Apr 2026-Mar 2027), so the next headwind is imminent.

docs.t: CLM-005017 successes_failures
docs.x: Takeda states that ENTYVIO, its top-selling product, will lose regulatory exclusivity in the latter half of this decade; certain Entyvio patents (formulation, dosing, manufacturing process) are expected to expire in 2032 and the exact timing of biosimilar entry is uncertain. Entyvio (21% of revenue) faces exclusivity loss while the subcutaneous pen and pediatric label expansions are meant to extend franchise life.

docs.t: CLM-005018 pipeline
docs.x: The subcutaneous ENTYVIO Pen was approved in the U.S. for ulcerative colitis in September 2023 and Crohn's disease in April 2024; the FDA accepted an sBLA for IV ENTYVIO in pediatric UC/CD (PDUFA Q1 CY2027). Formulation and label extension are Takeda's disclosed defence of Entyvio.

docs.t: CLM-005019 successes_failures
docs.x: TAKHZYRO's listed U.S. patent expiry is January 2036 (regulatory protection to March 2032) and no U.S. generic of GATTEX/REVESTIVE had launched as of March 2026, with market-entry timing uncertain.

docs.t: CLM-005020 successes_failures
docs.x: In June 2020 the FDA issued a warning letter for Takeda's Hikari plant (since closed after reclassification to Voluntary Action Indicated); remediation caused a Leuprorelin supply shortage, and a Delaware court found for AbbVie in December 2023 with a final damages award of USD 505 million including interest. A public manufacturing-quality event with a quantified cost; it is a documented operational risk for the manufacturing baseline.

docs.t: CLM-005021 partnerships_ma
docs.x: In FY2024 Takeda dissolved its Japanese generics joint venture with Teva, recognising a JPY 18.9bn impairment and receiving JPY 56.5bn (including JPY 50.8bn of dividends) on transfer in March 2025.

docs.t: CLM-005022 successes_failures
docs.x: Takeda recorded impairment charges of JPY 74.0bn on ALOFISEL after the ADMIRE-CD II Phase 3 topline and JPY 28.5bn on EXKIVITY after deciding to withdraw it globally (announced October 2023) in the year ended March 2024. Two recently launched products failed commercially or confirmatorily; both are documented value write-downs.

docs.t: CLM-005023 successes_failures
docs.x: Takeda stopped TAK-994 (narcolepsy, Phase 2) after a clinical hold, stating a data-driven decision to pivot to TAK-861 and other orexin molecules. The orexin franchise survived a failed first molecule; oveporexton's approval in 2026 followed the pivot.

docs.t: CLM-005024 successes_failures
docs.x: Takeda's Phase 3 SKYLINE (Dravet) and SKYWAY (LGS) studies of soticlestat missed primary endpoints in June 2024; after FDA feedback that the data package could not support an NDA, Takeda discontinued soticlestat on 30 January 2025, having impaired JPY 21.5bn of intangible assets. One of the late-stage failures within the 2021-2026 window.

docs.t: CLM-005025 successes_failures
docs.x: On 1 October 2025 Takeda announced it would discontinue all cell therapy efforts and seek an external partner for the platform, expecting a JPY 58.0bn impairment mainly for the gamma-delta T-cell platform; Fierce Biotech reported 137 Massachusetts roles affected. Takeda's cell therapy bets (GammaDelta acquisition in 2021, a Cambridge cell-therapy facility in 2020) were abandoned; its modality focus is now small molecules, biologics and ADCs.

docs.t: CLM-005026 successes_failures
docs.x: Takeda discontinued TAK-004 (an investigational peptide for nausea and vomiting) for strategic reasons at its FY2025 earnings on 13 May 2026.

docs.t: CLM-005027 pipeline
docs.x: Oveporexton (TAK-861, oral orexin-2 receptor agonist) met all primary and secondary endpoints at week 12 in the Phase 3 FirstLight and RadiantLight studies in narcolepsy type 1 at 1 mg and 2 mg twice daily (p<0.001). Company-reported; regulator labelling is in the approval claim below.

docs.t: CLM-005028 pipeline
docs.x: The two Phase 3 narcolepsy type 1 trials of TAK-861 in ClinicalTrials.gov are NCT06470828 (n=168, started 2024-07-02, completed) and NCT06505031 (n=105, started 2024-10-08, completed); the FDA states two 12-week studies enrolled 273 adults (168+105).

docs.t: CLM-005029 pipeline
docs.x: On 5 August 2026 the FDA approved Orzeyful (oveporexton) for narcolepsy type 1 in adults, with Breakthrough Therapy designation and Priority Review; the product is lawful to market after a DEA scheduling decision. First of three planned late-stage launches; launch revenue is not yet reported.

docs.t: CLM-005030 pipeline
docs.x: Oveporexton was filed in China (January 2026), the U.S. (February 2026, Priority Review, PDUFA Q3 CY2026) and Japan (March 2026, SAKIGAKE and orphan designation); the EU was in Phase 3 as of the 20-F table.

docs.t: CLM-005031 pipeline
docs.x: Rusfertide (TAK-121, hepcidin mimetic, licensed from Protagonist) met the VERIFY Phase 3 primary endpoint in polycythemia vera; NCT05210790 enrolled 293 adults and its lead sponsor in the registry is Protagonist Therapeutics.

docs.t: CLM-005032 pipeline
docs.x: On 28 August 2026 the FDA approved Mimrylo (rusfertide) for adults with polycythemia vera; per FDA, 76.9% of patients on Mimrylo required no phlebotomy in weeks 20-32 versus 32.9% on placebo in the 293-patient VERIFY study.

docs.t: CLM-005033 pipeline
docs.x: Zasocitinib (TAK-279, oral TYK2 inhibitor) met all co-primary and ranked secondary endpoints in Phase 3 LATITUDE PsO 3001 (NCT06088043, n=693) and 3002 (NCT06108544, n=1,108), with about 70% reaching sPGA 0/1 at week 16.

docs.t: CLM-005034 pipeline
docs.x: Takeda reported (June 2026) that zasocitinib was statistically superior to deucravacitinib on PASI 100 at week 16 (>35% responders) in the head-to-head LATITUDE Atlas study (NCT06973291, n=606, completed April 2026).

docs.t: CLM-005035 pipeline
docs.x: On 14 September 2026 Takeda announced FDA acceptance of the zasocitinib NDA under Priority Review for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and that the EMA accepted its marketing authorisation application; Takeda said the filing has no significant impact on its FY2026 forecast.

docs.t: CLM-005036 partnerships_ma
docs.x: Takeda acquired Nimbus Lakshmi, Inc. (TYK2 inhibitor TAK-279) in February 2023 for USD 4.0bn upfront plus two USD 1.0bn milestones payable at annual net sales of USD 4.0bn and USD 5.0bn. Largest public deal of the window; success now depends on zasocitinib's launch and competitive position against deucravacitinib and IL-23 agents.

docs.t: CLM-005037 pipeline
docs.x: Zasocitinib psoriatic arthritis Phase 3 studies are ongoing (NCT06671496 n=601 and NCT06671483 n=1,583, active, not recruiting; primary completion May 2027), with a further PsA study NCT07871721 not yet recruiting.

docs.t: CLM-005038 pipeline
docs.x: Mezagitamab (TAK-079, anti-CD38) is in Phase 3 for chronic primary ITP (NCT06722235, n=171 est., started 2025-02) and IgA nephropathy (NCT06963827, n=347 est., started 2025-07); Japan's MHLW granted orphan designation for ITP (June 2025) and IgAN (November 2025).

docs.t: CLM-005039 pipeline
docs.x: Fazirsiran (TAK-999, RNAi from Arrowhead) is in Phase 3 for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency-associated liver disease (NCT05677971, n=160 est., estimated primary completion January 2029). Readout timing sits beyond the FY2028 savings horizon.

docs.t: CLM-005040 pipeline
docs.x: Elritercept (TAK-226, activin ligand trap licensed from Keros) is in Phase 3 for anemia in lower-risk MDS (NCT06499285, n=225 est., started 2025-05) with additional Phase 3 starts in 2026 (e.g., NCT07422480 and NCT07623161 seen in registry search).

docs.t: CLM-005041 pipeline
docs.x: At its December 2024 R&D Day Takeda stated that its six late-stage programs (oveporexton, zasocitinib, rusfertide, mezagitamab, fazirsiran, elritercept) have combined potential peak revenue of USD 10-20bn, and repeated the figure in its November 2025 shareholder report. Treat as a company scenario, not a forecast; the range is wide (2x).

docs.t: CLM-005042 pipeline
docs.x: The December 2024 R&D Day plan was three Phase 3 readouts in 2025 (oveporexton, zasocitinib, rusfertide), with filings for those indications in FY2025-FY2026 and five further indication filings in FY2027-FY2029 including zasocitinib in psoriatic arthritis, mezagitamab, fazirsiran and elritercept. Delivery against the dated plan is the strongest public evidence of late-stage execution.

docs.t: CLM-005043 partnerships_ma
docs.x: In FY2025 Takeda licensed two late-stage oncology assets from Innovent Biologics (IBI363 PD-1/IL-2 bispecific, IBI343 Claudin 18.2 ADC) for worldwide rights outside China, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan; IBI363 is in Phase 3 for 2L squamous NSCLC and IBI343 in Phase 3 for 3L gastric cancer in Japan/China.

docs.t: CLM-005044 pipeline
docs.x: The FY2025 20-F lists Phase 3 or filed assets: oveporexton (filed JP/US/CN), rusfertide (filed US), zasocitinib (Phase 3 psoriasis, PsA, pediatric), mezagitamab (ITP, IgAN), fazirsiran, elritercept (MDS), mirvetuximab (Japan filed), IBI363/IBI343, plus ENTYVIO pediatric studies and TAK-227 (celiac, Phase 2b).

docs.t: CLM-005045 commercial_market_access
docs.x: QDENGA revenue was JPY 9.6bn in FY2023, JPY 35.6bn in FY2024 and JPY 40.8bn in FY2025 (+14.6% AER); the 7-year pivotal TIDES Phase 3 completed in November 2025 confirming sustained protection across all four serotypes; QDENGA is a 'New Launch' from FY2026. Dengue vaccine revenue remains small (<1% of revenue) and Qdenga economics are not disclosed beyond revenue.

docs.t: CLM-005046 scientific_rd
docs.x: Takeda describes an R&D transformation since 2014 to diversify modalities and engage innovation ecosystems through partnerships; its R&D focuses on GI and inflammation, neuroscience and oncology, with targeted investment in plasma-derived therapies (PDT); the FY2025 filing reports modality focus on small molecules, biologics and ADCs after exiting cell therapy. The model is portfolio-driven with heavy in-licensing; see partnership claims.

docs.t: CLM-005047 scientific_rd
docs.x: Takeda's R&D sites are Cambridge and Lexington (Massachusetts; global R&D headquarters, GI/inflammation, oncology), the Shonan Health Innovation Park in Japan (neuroscience research) and Vienna, Austria (biologics and PDT); a 15-year lease for a ~600,000 sq ft R&D facility in Kendall Square is planned for occupancy from 2026. San Diego was not mentioned in the passages read.

docs.t: CLM-005048 scientific_rd
docs.x: Takeda states oveporexton was discovered in its Shonan, Japan laboratories and that it is the world leader in orexin science. Oveporexton is an internally discovered asset, evidence that in-house discovery can still deliver a first-in-class molecule.

docs.t: CLM-005049 data_ai
docs.x: The FY2025 20-F lists research collaborations including Iambic Therapeutics (computational discovery engine), Nabla Bio (AI protein design), BridGene (chemoproteomics), Charles River Laboratories and the MIT-Takeda Program with MIT's J-Clinic for AI in drug development. Breadth of AI-enabled discovery partnerships is documented; their productivity is an EVIDENCE_GAP.

docs.t: CLM-005050 partnerships_ma
docs.x: The 20-F licensing table shows pipeline in-licensing or collaboration with Arrowhead (fazirsiran), Protagonist (rusfertide), Keros (elritercept), Innovent (IBI363/IBI343), AbbVie (mirvetuximab in Japan), Kumquat, COUR, Halozyme (ENHANZE for vedolizumab), Denali, Neurocrine and others. Four of the six late-stage programs (zasocitinib, rusfertide, elritercept, fazirsiran) originate outside Takeda; oveporexton and mezagitamab are Takeda-originated per this evidence (interpretation).

docs.t: CLM-005051 leadership
docs.x: Andrew Plump has been Takeda's President of R&D (a Director) and joined in 2015 as Chief Medical and Scientific Officer; he came from Sanofi (SVP research and translational medicine).

docs.t: CLM-005052 partnerships_ma
docs.x: Takeda Ventures, the Center for External Innovation and any stated share of external pipeline were not found in the FY2025 20-F text or captured web pages (searches returned no hits).
