docs.t: CLM-002053 commercial_market_access
docs.x: FDA approved TREMFYA for adult Crohn's disease in March 2025 (IV and subcutaneous induction; GALAXI showed superiority to Stelara on pooled endoscopic endpoints per J&J), and trade press framed it as positioning Tremfya as Stelara's successor; Cigna/Evernorth had announced in September 2024 a $0 out-of-pocket Stelara copycat for 2025. Payer-controlled private-label biosimilars (Nuvaila, Cordavis, Quallent) are a distinct erosion channel for Stelara beyond clinical substitution.

docs.t: CLM-002054 policy_regulation
docs.x: CMS's fact sheet states that negotiated Maximum Fair Prices for 10 Part D drugs (a list that includes STELARA, XARELTO and IMBRUVICA per J&J's 10-K) take effect on 2026-01-01; per-drug MFP values and J&J's financial impact were not verified in this research.

docs.t: CLM-002055 pipeline
docs.x: ClinicalTrials.gov lists a Phase 3 program for icotrokinra (JNJ-77242113) beyond psoriasis: psoriatic arthritis (NCT06807424 start 2025-01-09, n=813; NCT06878404 start 2025-02-21, n=552), ulcerative colitis (NCT07196748, start 2025-10-01, n=896) and a Phase 2/3 Crohn's study (NCT07196722, start 2025-10-03, n=1,092); the adolescent/adult plaque psoriasis Phase 3 NCT06095115 (n=684) had primary completion 2024-07-29. J&J is extending an oral IL-23-receptor peptide across psoriasis, PsA, UC and CD, the same indications that anchor TREMFYA/STELARA, which is consistent with a successor-franchise strategy (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002056 successes_failures

Pasritamig and bleximenib are still pre-readout; their contribution to the '2030 blockbuster' ambition is unverified.

docs.t: CLM-002060 financials
docs.x: In Q3 2026 (quarter reported 2026-10-13) J&J's reported sales were USD 25,399m (+5.9%; operational +6.0%): Innovative Medicine USD 16,757m (+7.7%; STELARA a ~690 basis-point drag) and MedTech USD 8,642m (+2.5%); net earnings were USD 210m (EPS USD 0.09 vs USD 2.12) after a special charge for the proposed talc resolution and M&A items. MedTech growth (2.5%) is below Innovative Medicine (7.7%) in the latest quarter, consistent with the Orthopaedics-separation rationale (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002061 financials
docs.x: J&J raised its FY2026 guidance on 2026-10-13 to estimated reported sales of USD 101.0-101.4bn (midpoint USD 101.2bn, +7.4%) and adjusted EPS of USD 11.05-11.15 (midpoint USD 11.10), and said it has 'clearer line of sight to double-digit growth by the end of the decade'. A statement of expectation; outcome unverified.

docs.t: CLM-002062 successes_failures
docs.x: On 2026-07-27 J&J announced a proposed comprehensive resolution of ovarian talc litigation (about 76,000 claims) with a USD 5.5bn commitment, first payment no more than USD 3bn in 2027, conditional on at least 95% participation; it follows a 2026-07-22 MDL order to show cause on specific causation, and J&J says it will retain talc liabilities and has indemnified Kenvue.

docs.t: CLM-002063 successes_failures
docs.x: Reuters/CNBC reported that plaintiffs' firms confirmed the 2026-07-27 deal, that it needs 95% participation, that it covers existing but not future claims, and that a lead plaintiffs' lawyer (Chris Seeger) said J&J could ultimately pay USD 7bn or more because per-claim values are not capped. Total cost range USD 5.5bn+ (company) to USD 7bn+ (plaintiff counsel estimate); the 10-K reserve at FY2025 end was ~USD 3.4bn (CLM-002016).

docs.t: CLM-002064 leadership
docs.x: J&J announced on 2026-08-04 that Jennifer Taubert (EVP, Worldwide Chairman Innovative Medicine since 2018) will retire and be succeeded effective 2026-09-01 by Tom Cavanaugh (joined J&J 2017, previously Celgene; most recently Company Group Chairman, North America), who joins the Executive Committee. Leadership change in the Innovative Medicine segment head occurs as the Stelara cliff is absorbed and ICOTYDE launches (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002065 pipeline
docs.x: The FDA approved ICOTYDE (icotrokinra), an oral IL-23 receptor antagonist peptide, for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in adults and pediatric patients 12+ (>=40 kg) on or about 2026-03-17/18; J&J reports head-to-head superiority studies with about 70% achieving IGA 0/1 and 55% PASI 90 at Week 16 and says four Phase 3 studies in about 2,500 patients met all primary endpoints. First U.S. approval of an oral IL-23-receptor peptide arrives about 14 months after the first U.S. Stelara biosimilar launch (2025-01) and adds a second IL-23 franchise beside TREMFYA (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002066 robotics_automation
docs.x: On 2024-08-02 J&J MedTech/DePuy Synthes announced that the VELYS Spine active robotic-assisted and navigation system, developed with eCential Robotics, had received FDA 510(k) clearance for planning and instrumenting cervical, thoracolumbar and sacroiliac fusion, with commercial availability expected in the first half of 2025. The 10-K's only VELYS-linked outcome is 'pull through' for ATTUNE knees (CLM-002029); no spine adoption or placement numbers were found (gap).

docs.t: CLM-002067 robotics_automation
docs.x: J&J MedTech reported that the company-sponsored, single-arm TARGET study of the MONARCH bronchoscopy platform (679 patients, 21 sites; published in CHEST 2025-04-26) reached the lesion in 98.7% of cases with a diagnostic yield of 83.2% and a safety profile it describes as comparable to non-robotic bronchoscopy. MONARCH has an outcome dataset, but a single-arm design does not show superiority over competing robotic bronchoscopes (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002068 partnerships_ma
docs.x: At completion of the Shockwave acquisition (2024-05-31) J&J described Shockwave as offering the first and only commercially available intravascular lithotripsy platform for coronary and peripheral artery disease, expected it to become MedTech's thirteenth USD 1bn+ priority platform, and guided to about USD 0.10 (2024) and USD 0.17 (2025) adjusted-EPS dilution. The stated platform threshold was met in 2025 per the 10-K figures, while the EPS dilution outturn was not checked (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002069 policy_regulation
docs.x: On 2025-06-27 U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras ruled that HRSA did not act unlawfully in requiring J&J to obtain approval before implementing a rebate model for 340B-discounted drugs, rejecting J&J's claim that HRSA lacked authority for prior approval; STAT reported that J&J's remedy was lost, and a different judge had reached the same result in suits by Lilly, BMS and Novartis a month earlier. J&J's unilateral rebate path is closed unless HRSA approves; the contract-pharmacy delivery policy remains the lever it asserts (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002070 policy_regulation
docs.x: A U.S. District Court in Maine issued a preliminary injunction on 2025-12-29 pausing HRSA's 340B rebate pilot (10 drugs in year one) that was due to start 2026-01-01; HFMA's later update reports HHS stepping back from its appeal. Even the government-run rebate route was blocked, so the manufacturer-rebate model J&J sought has not been implemented as of the sources read (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002071 patient_care
docs.x: J&J's U.S. patient support programme, Janssen CarePath, is being renamed J&J withMe; the company page lists cost support for eligible commercially insured patients, free trial products, referral to independent foundations, patient assistance for uninsured or under-covered patients, and benefit verification for providers. Patient-support design is standard industry hub-and-copay infrastructure; its effect on Stelara-to-Tremfya conversion is not evidenced (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002072 competitive_advantage
docs.x: DARZALEX, CARVYKTI, TECVAYLI and TALVEY, the four multiple-myeloma brands in J&J's FY2025 oncology table, together recorded USD 17,371m of 2025 sales (USD 14,351m + 1,887m + 670m + 463m), about 18.4% of J&J's USD 94,193m total. Franchise depth across antibody (CD38), CAR-T and two bispecifics is a moat candidate: replicating it needs a CD38 antibody, a BCMA CAR-T supply chain and bispecific platforms, each a multi-year effort (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002073 successes_failures
docs.x: DARZALEX alone was about 15.2% of J&J's FY2025 sales (USD 14,351m of USD 94,193m), and DARZALEX plus TREMFYA, ERLEADA and IMBRUVICA accounted for about USD 25.9bn. Concentration is rising as Stelara declines; DARZALEX's patent and biosimilar timelines were not researched here and are the main open vulnerability (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-002074 competitive_advantage
docs.x: J&J's FY2025 segment data show MedTech earning a 12.2% segment pre-tax margin against 36.9% in Innovative Medicine, while J&J's own 2024 Shockwave release asserts the pairing of Abiomed (heart recovery), Biosense Webster (electrophysiology) and Shockwave makes it a category leader in four large cardiovascular markets. The 'dual platform' advantage is unproven: the two segments share a balance sheet and cardiovascular focus (e.g. Xarelto, Impella) but no disclosed revenue synergy; the October 2025 Orthopaedics separation implies management sees portfolio focus as worth more than breadth (HYPOTHESIS).

docs.t: CLM-002075 successes_failures
docs.x: Excluding STELARA, J&J's total sales rose from about USD 78.5bn in FY2024 (88,821 - 10,361) to about USD 88.1bn in FY2025 (94,193 - 6,078), about +12.3%, compared with +6.0% reported growth for the group. Underlying growth ex-Stelara is about double the reported rate, of which about 1 point is acquired (INTERPRETATION).

docs.t: CLM-007000 Zepbound tirzepatide commercial_market_access
docs.x: In August 2024 Lilly began selling Zepbound 2.5 mg and 5 mg single-dose vials through a new self-pay pharmacy component of LillyDirect at $399 and $549 per four-week supply, saying this was less than half the list price of other obesity incretins. docs.t: CLM-007001 Zepbound commercial_market_access
docs.x: On 25 February 2025 Lilly announced the launch of 7.5 mg and 10 mg Zepbound single-dose vials at $499 under a new Zepbound Self Pay Journey Program (search snippet only; page not opened).

docs.t: CLM-007002 Zepbound commercial_market_access
docs.x: On 1 December 2025 Lilly cut LillyDirect self-pay prices for Zepbound single-dose vials: 2.5 mg from $349 to $299, 5 mg from $499 to $399, and 7.5 mg to 15 mg from $499 to $449 per month under the Self Pay Journey Program; the release states non-program prices of $599 (7.5 mg), $699 (10 mg), $849 (12.5 mg) and $1,049 (15 mg). Three list-to-cash price cuts in 16 months (Aug 2024 entry price $399 -> Dec 2025 $299) show the cash price is being used as a competitive lever alongside the November 2025 US government agreement (CLM-001036).

docs.t: CLM-007003 Walmart commercial_market_access
docs.x: LillyDirect and Walmart announced a collaboration (search-index date 29 Oct 2025) to let Zepbound self-pay vials be picked up at Walmart pharmacies nationwide by mid-November 2025, with Walmart described as having nearly 4,600 pharmacies; lowest dose then at $349 per month. Lilly kept the cash price outside insurance but borrowed a retail pharmacy footprint, which blunts the criticism that DTC channels need home delivery only.

docs.t: CLM-007004 Zepbound KwikPen commercial_market_access

docs.t: CLM-007005 commercial_market_access

docs.t: CLM-007009 policy_regulation

The channel is time-limited by its own agreements, which matters for any company building a capability around it.

docs.t: CLM-007010 policy_regulation

Limits how much volume a cash channel can take from insured patients.

docs.t: CLM-007011 Zepbound Wegovy commercial_market_access

docs.x: CVS Health announced on 5 May 2026 that from 1 July 2026 its most common commercial template formularies would prefer the interchangeable Stelara biosimilars Pyzchiva and Yesintek over Stelara, with most members paying $0, and would add biosimilar-based preferences in multiple sclerosis (Tysabri) and rare blood disorders (Soliris). Stelara's net price erosion continues into 2026 through formulary exclusion, in addition to the Part D negotiated price.

docs.t: CLM-007016 Cordavis Quallent Nuvaila commercial_market_access
docs.x: Drug Channels reports that by July 2025 nine Stelara biosimilars plus one unbranded J&J biologic were on the US market with list prices 5% to 90% below Stelara, that four of the nine were marketed by PBM-affiliated private-label businesses, that Optum Rx excluded Stelara from two main formularies from 1 July 2025, and that the CMS maximum fair price for Stelara for 2026 is 66% below its 2023 list price. PBM-owned private labels (Cordavis, Quallent, Nuvaila) turned the second large biologic LOE into a vertically integrated formulary decision.

docs.t: CLM-007017 Stelara Tremfya commercial_market_access
docs.x: J&J's FY2025 10-K states that Stelara was about 6.5% of total revenue in fiscal 2025, that US Stelara sales were about $3.8 billion, that Immunology sales of $15.7 billion fell 11.8% mainly because of Stelara biosimilar competition and Medicare Part D redesign, and that the Stelara decline reduced worldwide Innovative Medicine growth by about 10.4 percentage points. Second-largest product lost roughly one-tenth of segment growth in a year; Tremfya share gains have not yet offset it at segment level.

docs.t: CLM-007018 commercial_market_access
docs.x: J&J's FY2025 10-K attributes sales effects to Medicare Part D redesign: reductions for Erleada, Invega Sustenna/Trinza, Opsumit and Uptravi, and a benefit to Xarelto sales growth; Stelara and Xarelto were selected in the first IRA negotiation list with Medicare prices applying from 2026. Part D redesign shifts liability to manufacturers in the catastrophic phase, so drugs with high Medicare mix lose and some with low list price gain.

docs.t: CLM-007019 commercial_market_access
docs.x: AbbVie's FY2025 10-K reports provisions for rebates and chargebacks of $65.1 billion in 2025, $59.3 billion in 2024 and $56.8 billion in 2023, with managed-care rebates, Medicaid/Medicare rebates and wholesaler chargebacks making up about 94% of the 2025 total, against net revenues of $61.2 billion in 2025. (computed) Provisions equal about 1.06x net revenue in 2025, i.e. gross sales were roughly 2.06x net revenue before other deductions; this is the closest public gross-to-net proxy for AbbVie.

docs.t: CLM-007020 Skyrizi Rinvoq Humira commercial_market_access

docs.t: CLM-007029 commercial_market_access
docs.x: J&J's FY2025 10-K shows worldwide sales of $1,887 million for Carvykti (2024: $963 million, attributed to share gains and capacity expansion), $1,696 million for Spravato (2024: $1,077 million, attributed to increased physician and patient demand) and $5,155 million for Tremfya (2024: $3,670 million, attributed to share gains and market growth). docs.t: CLM-007030 patient_care
docs.x: FDA's Spravato REMS document states Spravato is available only through a restricted distribution program because of risks of sedation, dissociation, respiratory depression, abuse and misuse, is intended for use only in a certified healthcare setting, and must never be dispensed directly to a patient for home use. Spravato growth required certifying treatment sites; its distribution constraint is regulatory, not a choice, and it cuts against the home-administration trend.

docs.x: Lilly's FY2025 10-K table shows Mounjaro revenue of $22,965 million in 2025 versus $11,540 million in 2024 and Zepbound $13,542 million versus $4,926 million; Mounjaro and Zepbound were 56 percent of total Lilly revenue.

docs.t: CLM-007032 commercial_market_access
docs.x: Search snippets (BioPharma Dive, pharmaphorum) state Kisunla sales were $21 million in Q1 2025 and that an FDA-cleared modified dosing regimen (July 2025) carries a lower risk of adverse reactions that may have held back uptake; neither page could be opened. Reasons for slow uptake (MRI monitoring, ARIA risk, diagnosis pathway) are plausible but not verified here.

docs.t: CLM-007035 patient_care

docs.t: CLM-007044 Zepbound KwikPen patient_care
docs.x: Lilly said in February 2026 that FDA approved a label expansion for Zepbound to include a four-dose single-patient-use KwikPen delivering a month of treatment, available through LillyDirect self-pay from $299 per month alongside single-dose vials.

docs.t: CLM-007045 patient_care
docs.x: Pear Therapeutics, a prescription digital therapeutics company, filed for Chapter 11 on 7 April 2023, suspended new prescriptions, laid off most of its 200 staff and its CEO stepped down; its former CEO blamed payers' ability to deny payment, and a 2022 company forecast of $14-16 million revenue preceded the filing. Industry calibration: a digital therapeutic with RCT evidence still failed on payment, so pharma adoption of standalone DTx is a reimbursement problem before it is a product problem.

docs.t: CLM-007046 patient_care

docs.t: CLM-007047 patient_care

Claims about decentralized-trial maturity need a different source set (trial registry, publications).

docs.t: CLM-007049 commercial_market_access

docs.t: CLM-007050 commercial_market_access

docs.t: CLM-007052 commercial_market_access
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: A US cash-pay direct-to-patient channel on the LillyDirect model fits Takeda poorly: its main products are infused or specialty-distributed biologics and plasma therapies sold through payer coverage and hubs, and the evidence shows self-pay scaling in a category (obesity) with no insurance coverage for many patients and vial/pen products priced at $299-$449 per month. Capability baseline class 14 (patient services / market access) is an EVIDENCE_GAP; a cash channel is not a priority for GI, rare, PDT or vaccines.

docs.t: CLM-007053 patient_care
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Home/subcutaneous conversion is the best-evidenced transferable mechanism for Takeda, because Entyvio SC is already approved in three regions and described as driving uptake, comparable moves (Tremfya SC share gains; Zepbound pens) coincide with strong growth, and Entyvio faces Medicare negotiation in 2028. Maps to baseline class 1 (GI/immunology franchise, EXISTING_STRENGTH) and class 8 (launch execution, POTENTIAL_NEW_CAPABILITY).

docs.t: CLM-007054 commercial_market_access
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: PBM private-label and formulary exclusivity dynamics seen in Humira, Stelara and Zepbound/Wegovy are a direct threat to Takeda's GI franchise if an Entyvio biosimilar or a preferred competitor arrives, so Takeda needs payer-contracting depth (rebate-for-access, interchangeable biosimilar defense) more than new channels. Baseline class 1 (EXISTING_STRENGTH) and class 7 (LOE replacement, EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED).

docs.t: CLM-007055 patient_care
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: The Spravato REMS and Carvykti capacity examples are the closest analogues to launches in Takeda's neuroscience (oveporexton), oncology and rare portfolio: they show launch pace governed by site certification or manufacturing capacity, which argues for pre-launch investment in site networks and supply. Baseline class 8 (new-brand launch execution, POTENTIAL_NEW_CAPABILITY) and class 3 (rare disease / orexin).

docs.t: CLM-007056 patient_care
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Takeda's plasma-derived therapies suit device-led home administration (HYHUB) and site-of-care shifts more than DTC or loyalty models; AbbVie's Allē loyalty and Lilly's cash channel do not transfer to rare-disease and PDT products. Baseline class 2 (plasma network and PDT manufacturing, EXISTING_STRENGTH) and class 3.

docs.t: CLM-007057 patient_care
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Pear's failure suggests Takeda should treat standalone digital therapeutics as a payment-evidence risk and prefer digital features attached to a drug (reminders, nurse support) over separately reimbursed apps. Baseline class 14 (patient services) and class 9 (data platform).

docs.t: CLM-007058 patient_care
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Takeda's baseline records patient services and market access as an EVIDENCE_GAP (CLM-005072); this shard confirms public Takeda disclosures give only a cumulative Help at Hand count and no adherence or hub-performance data, so any recommendation to expand support programs must be labelled an assumption pending internal validation (IVB-013). Baseline class 14.

docs.t: CLM-011039 strategy
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: TSMC's mechanism is a neutral dedicated manufacturer that does not sell competing products, funds leading-edge capacity (2026 capex guidance US$52-56 billion) and builds an ecosystem of partner-supplied design tooling (Open Innovation Platform since 2008), so customers can design for its process.

docs.t: CLM-011040 strategy
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: The TSMC analogy breaks for pharma because a CDMO serves many sponsors but sponsors guard process know-how and safety liability, patents are held by sponsors, and plasma fractionation carries donor-supply and regulatory constraints that wafers do not.

docs.t: CLM-011041 strategy
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Takeda could test a neutral-capacity role in plasma (toll fractionation or shared analytics for other plasma-product companies) if network utilisation shows spare capacity after the Los Angeles expansion, but capacity data, competitive sensitivities and regulatory feasibility are unknown.

docs.t: CLM-011042 strategy
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: AWS shows an internal infrastructure capability turned into an external service business that now earns about 57% of Amazon operating income, built on a broad set of on-demand services sold to developers and enterprises.

docs.t: CLM-011043 strategy
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: The AWS analogy predicts that the first pharma internal capability to be productised for outsiders is one with standalone cost advantage and external demand; Lilly TuneLab (federated models for biotechs, Benchling distribution to 1,300+ customers) is the closest case and is operational with no uptake outcome disclosed.

docs.t: CLM-011044 strategy
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: The AWS analogy breaks for pharma because AWS customers were not competitors of Amazon's retail unit in most cases, whereas pharma's buyers are rivals who may avoid dependence on a competitor's platform, and because a pharma's data is constrained by consent and privacy rules.

docs.t: CLM-011045 strategy
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Takeda should not attempt to productise internal capabilities to third parties until an internal capability has measured cost or speed advantage, because its public record contains no deployed AI or automation outcome (IVB-001, IVB-002).

docs.t: CLM-011046 strategy
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Intuitive Surgical's mechanism is an installed base of about 11,106 systems that generates instruments, service and lease revenue per procedure (recurring revenue 84% of revenue in 2025) and training and data advantages that raise switching costs for hospitals.

docs.t: CLM-011047 strategy
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: The Intuitive analogy breaks for pharma robotics because J&J's robotics entry has cost an impairment of USD 0.9 billion on OTTAVA (Auris, fiscal 2021), OTTAVA has one announced installation, and an installed-base moat needs years and hospital capital budgets that a drug company does not control.

docs.t: CLM-011048 commercial_market_access
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Takeda gets Intuitive-style pull-through more cheaply from drug-device combinations it already ships (Entyvio pen, HYHUB for Hyqvia) than from surgical or lab robotics, because the installed base is patients on therapy and the economics are consumable-like.

docs.t: CLM-011049 partnerships_ma
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: The Roche-Flatiron case shows a pharma company buying a data and workflow platform (USD 1.9 billion) and deliberately keeping it a separate legal entity with segregated data so that other pharma customers (14 of the top 15 oncology companies in 2018) continue to use it.

docs.t: CLM-011050 partnerships_ma
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: The Flatiron analogy breaks for Takeda because Flatiron is an oncology-specific EHR and real-world-evidence asset built over years inside US community oncology networks, while Takeda's core areas (GI, rare, plasma, neuroscience) have no equivalent data network and the 2018 outcome was not re-verified in this review.

docs.t: CLM-011051 partnerships_ma
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: A neutral real-world data asset in a rare or plasma-treated disease (registries with patient organisations and health systems) could be a data moat for Takeda only if built or bought as a neutral entity, because competitors will not contribute data to a platform owned by a direct rival.

docs.t: CLM-011052 data_ai
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Among Lilly, J&J and AbbVie the deployed data assets are Lilly TuneLab (operational, launched 2025-09-09), AbbVie ARCH (operational, built by fewer than ten staff plus contractors), J&J Polyphonic (early access, select hospitals only) and the five-company federated OpenFold3 effort (pilot); none has independent outcome evidence.

docs.t: CLM-011053 data_ai
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Takeda's public data and AI baseline is EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED: a Databricks-hosted agent platform for 10,000+ employees (vendor-hosted, self-reported), 80% of the digital workforce external at design time, AISB membership since October 2025 but absence from the AISB Bind founding list, and no quantified AI outcome.

docs.t: CLM-011054 data_ai
docs.x: RECOMMENDATION (EVIDENCE_BACKED): Keep participating in federated, multi-company model consortia (AISB) for structure and property prediction and decide on follow-on tasks such as AISB Bind from measured value, because federation lets Takeda use pooled information without surrendering raw data and Takeda cannot match Lilly's data volume alone.

docs.t: CLM-011055 data_ai
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: A single governed cross-franchise R&D data layer (an ARCH-type knowledge graph with a decision to reuse de-identified trial data for all R&D) would raise reuse of Takeda's own trial and real-world data, if the current data estate is fragmented as AbbVie's was; the fragmentation is not known for Takeda.

docs.t: CLM-011056 data_ai
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Takeda's plasma operations (270+ centers with adaptive donor nomograms, immunoglobulins 18% of FY2025 revenue) generate donor, yield and process data that no competitor in the set holds; if captured and modelled it could be the one proprietary data class Takeda owns, but yield-per-center and cost-per-litre data are not public (IVB-006).

docs.t: CLM-011057 scientific_rd
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: In AI-enabled discovery every competitor deal found is at concept or prototype stage (Isomorphic, Chai, Nabla, Iambic, BigHat); the only demonstrated outcomes are negative or small: Recursion ended four of 11 programmes in 2025 and Insilico's rentosertib Phase IIa (71 patients) showed an FVC signal with liver-related discontinuations.

docs.t: CLM-011058 pipeline
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Takeda's window approvals and filings come from conventional routes: oveporexton from in-house orexin science (approved 2026-08-05), rusfertide in-licensed from Protagonist (approved 2026-08-28) and zasocitinib bought with Nimbus for USD 4.0 billion upfront (NDA planned 2026); Takeda exited cell therapy in October 2025 with a JPY 58.2bn impairment.

docs.t: CLM-011059 partnerships_ma
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Competitors are entering new modalities by acquisition or option rather than internal build: AbbVie bought Capstan (in vivo CAR-T, USD 2.1 billion) and took an siRNA option with ADARx (USD 335 million upfront); Lilly bought Verve (gene editing) and POINT (radioligands); J&J bought Ambrx (ADC) and Halda.

docs.t: CLM-011060 scientific_rd
docs.x: RECOMMENDATION (EVIDENCE_BACKED): Keep AI-discovery partnerships (Nabla, Iambic) in a milestone-gated structure with go/no-go decisions tied to first-in-human data before scaling spend, because no AI-platform deal in the competitor set has an independent clinical outcome and AI-origin programmes show ordinary attrition.

docs.t: CLM-011061 partnerships_ma
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Takeda could acquire exposure to one or two new modalities through option agreements, as AbbVie did with ADARx, in areas adjacent to existing assets (for example RNAi next to fazirsiran), instead of an acquisition, if the option fee is small relative to the USD 4.0 billion paid for Nimbus; the value of option structures to AbbVie is not yet realised.

docs.t: CLM-011062 robotics_automation
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: On the staged ladder, stages 1-2 (assisted and automated high-throughput work) are operational and commodity; stage 3 (integrated smart lab linking AI planning to owned wet labs) is prototype to pilot with vendor claims only (Nabla 3-4 week design-to-test, BigHat, the concept-stage Lilly-NVIDIA lab); stage 4 (bounded autonomous experimentation) and stage 5 (scaled automation) have no independent demonstration in any source opened.

docs.t: CLM-011063 robotics_automation
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Owned or venture-funded automation ventures have ended in divestment or distressed sale: Lilly's Life Sciences Studio went to the CRO Arctoris in 2024 (reason undisclosed; the 2020 start and Strateos link are unsupported per audit) and Zymergen sold to Ginkgo for about USD 300 million, one-tenth of its IPO valuation; the CRO service model continues.

docs.t: CLM-011064 robotics_automation
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Takeda has no public evidence of lab automation, continuous manufacturing or manufacturing robotics (EVIDENCE_GAP, IVB-002); its automation-relevant assets are the plasma network (233 to 275 centers over FY2022-FY2024) and a USD 230 million Los Angeles fractionation expansion adding up to 2 million litres per year.

docs.t: CLM-011065 robotics_automation
docs.x: RECOMMENDATION (EVIDENCE_BACKED): Obtain automated data generation as a service from CROs and cloud labs (the model that survived at Arctoris) instead of building an owned robotic lab, and review the position when an independent outcome from a competitor's autonomous-lab programme appears.

docs.t: CLM-011066 robotics_automation
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Takeda should set explicit triggers for moving up the automation ladder: an independent result from the Lilly-NVIDIA lab, first-in-human data from the Nabla programme, and a measured cost-per-experiment benchmark from a CRO pilot; absent these, stage 3 or higher investment is not supported by public evidence.

docs.t: CLM-011067 patient_care
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Competitor care-delivery moves are access or convenience moves with company-reported counts and no outcome data: LillyDirect (over 1 million patients in 2025, company-reported), Zepbound vials and KwikPen, J&J withMe, AbbVie Allē (over 6 million members) and Takeda Help at Hand (over 100,000 patients cumulative); no adherence, persistence or time-to-therapy result was found for any.

docs.t: CLM-011068 patient_care
docs.x: RECOMMENDATION (EVIDENCE_BACKED): Continue converting infused or vial-based therapies to subcutaneous and home administration with devices (Entyvio SC pen, HYHUB needle-free transfer for Hyqvia), the best-evidenced transferable care-delivery mechanism for Takeda's GI and PDT mix.

docs.t: CLM-011069 patient_care
docs.x: RECOMMENDATION (EVIDENCE_BACKED): Attach digital support to the drug (reminders, nurse support) instead of launching separately reimbursed digital therapeutics, because Pear Therapeutics filed for bankruptcy in April 2023 despite published evidence when reimbursement stalled.

docs.t: CLM-011070 patient_care
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Launch-pathway partnerships (diagnosis and certified-site networks for oveporexton in narcolepsy type 1) could govern launch speed more than promotion, as site certification governed Spravato and capacity governed Carvykti; whether oveporexton needs a restricted network is not established.

docs.t: CLM-011071 commercial_market_access
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Payer and policy exposure shape commercial models more than AI: CVS Caremark swapped Zepbound for Wegovy in July 2025 and restored it in October 2026; Stelara was moved behind interchangeable biosimilars from July 2026; AbbVie booked USD 65.1 billion of rebate and chargeback provisions in 2025; CMS selected Entyvio for Medicare price negotiation effective 2028.

docs.t: CLM-011072 commercial_market_access
docs.x: RECOMMENDATION (EVIDENCE_BACKED): Build payer-contracting and formulary-defence depth for Entyvio before biosimilar or preferred-competitor entry, using the Humira (rebate-for-access, co-branded supply) and Stelara (PBM template switch) cases as templates; the Entyvio IV/SC mix and biosimilar timing are unknown (IVB-004).

docs.t: CLM-011073 commercial_market_access
docs.x: RECOMMENDATION (EVIDENCE_BACKED): Do not copy a US cash-pay direct-to-patient channel: copay accumulator and anti-kickback rules restrict combining discounts with insurance and Takeda's infused, specialty and plasma products are sold through payer coverage and hubs.

docs.t: CLM-011074 commercial_market_access
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: AI decision support for field and medical teams (a J&J-style sales assistant and provider-insights tool) can be piloted at low compliance risk if it advises humans and does not generate or send promotional content; competitor deployments (AskJIA, Engagement.AI in 14 countries) report no usage or outcome data, so the benefit for Takeda is unproven.

docs.t: CLM-011075 partnerships_ma
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Takeda's window pattern is one flagship asset purchase (Nimbus, USD 4.0 billion upfront), then licences, options and equity (Protagonist, Keros, Innovent with USD 1.2 billion upfront including USD 100 million equity), divestitures and write-offs; Takeda states there were no significant acquisitions in the three years to March 2026, whereas AbbVie and J&J made multiple USD 8-17 billion purchases.

docs.t: CLM-011076 partnerships_ma
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Ecosystem arms differ in evidence: Lilly Catalyze360 bundles capital, lab space, development expertise and TuneLab; J&J is closing JLABS sites (Houston, Toronto, Washington DC, New York reported); Takeda's Center for External Innovation sits on the BaseLaunch board and its Ventures scope is not public (founding-date conflict also unresolved for AbbVie Ventures).

docs.t: CLM-011077 partnerships_ma
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Takeda could extend its ecosystem footprint cheaply by taking a larger role in shared venture-creation vehicles (BaseLaunch) instead of building its own incubator network, given J&J's retreat from JLABS sites and Takeda's undisclosed Ventures scope; outcomes of BaseLaunch companies were not assessed.

docs.t: CLM-011078 data_ai
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: People and operating-model evidence is thin: J&J reports 47,000 employees completed a required generative-AI course (a training metric, not a deployment) and a 10-15% share of use cases driving about 80% of value; AbbVie built ARCH with fewer than ten staff plus contractors; Takeda reports an 80% external digital workforce at design time and large-scale insourcing.

docs.t: CLM-011079 leadership
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Takeda is changing its cost base and leadership at the same time: a March 2026 transformation targets over JPY 200bn gross annual savings by FY2028 (restructuring cost JPY 150bn, 170bn, then 160bn in successive company figures; trade press reported about 4,500 role reductions), and Julie Kim became CEO on 24 June 2026; the share of savings attributable to technology versus other levers is unknown (IVB-003).

docs.t: CLM-011080 data_ai
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Takeda would learn faster from a small set of AI use cases measured against a pre-agreed baseline and pruned early, following the reported J&J reallocation of AI ownership to departments after a 900-case review, than from a broad rollout; J&J's result is a single-interview, self-reported claim.

docs.t: CLM-011081 leadership
docs.x: HYPOTHESIS: Pairing the JPY 200bn efficiency programme with a published reskilling and redeployment plan for roles touched by automation would reduce execution risk, if Takeda measures capability (tasks performed with AI tools) instead of course completions; the workforce effect of AI at Takeda is not publicly quantified.

docs.t: CLM-011082 data_ai
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Data moat: the strongest competitor example is Lilly TuneLab, a federated platform on Lilly data (company-estimated cost over USD 1 billion) with partners adding data; it is operational, distribution via Benchling is at pilot, and there is no independent outcome evidence.

docs.t: CLM-011083 robotics_automation
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Learning moat: the best evidenced competitor example is J&J's MONARCH, whose software-updatable design produced a third launch in 18 months with AI nodule segmentation (510(k) clearance announced 2026-08-17), but installed base and outcome data are undisclosed.

docs.t: CLM-011084 competitive_advantage
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: IP moat: the strongest competitor examples are Lilly's tirzepatide compound patent to 2036 and AbbVie's settlement-based entry dates (Humira biosimilar entry negotiated to 2023; Rinvoq generic entry not expected before April 2037).

docs.t: CLM-011085 business
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Infrastructure moat: the strongest competitor example is Lilly's incretin manufacturing build (Lebanon site raised to USD 9 billion, USD 21 billion of Indiana commitments since 2020) plus the LillyPod cluster; announced capacity is not operating capacity and the Medicine Foundry is at concept stage.

docs.t: CLM-011086 commercial_market_access
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Workflow-integration moat: the strongest competitor example is AbbVie's rebate-for-access contracting that kept at least 97% of adalimumab volume through March 2024 and its co-branded supply to CVS Caremark/Cordavis; the PBM template risk shows the same lever can be removed (Stelara, Zepbound).

docs.t: CLM-011087 data_ai
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Network-effects moat: the nearest competitor evidence is federated sharing, where TuneLab partners add data to Lilly-led models and the AISB consortium pooled over 20,000 private structures for a measured gain; neither shows a revenue effect and open model weights limit exclusivity.

docs.t: CLM-011088 robotics_automation
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Regulatory-experience moat: the strongest competitor example is J&J's first FDA De Novo for a table-integrated soft-tissue robot (OTTAVA, 2026-07-22), though completed installation is not shown; Takeda's own record includes a June 2020 FDA warning letter at Hikari that led to a supply shortage.

docs.t: CLM-011089 partnerships_ma
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Ecosystem moat: the strongest competitor example is Lilly Catalyze360 (Ventures, Gateway Labs, ExploR&D, TuneLab) with 1,300+ Benchling customers as a channel, set against J&J's reported JLABS site closures; no ecosystem arm has outcome evidence.

docs.t: CLM-011090 scientific_rd
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Academic partnerships: Takeda lists the MIT-Takeda Program with MIT J-Clinic for AI in drug development and Charles River among its research collaborations; no outcome is disclosed, and the usual mode is partner or license.

docs.t: CLM-011091 partnerships_ma
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Biotech precedents: Takeda acquired Nimbus (USD 4.0 billion upfront; Phase 3 positive, NDA planned) and in-licensed rusfertide (approved 2026-08-28); AbbVie bought Cerevel and wrote down USD 4.5 billion after emraclidine failed; licence-and-option deals carry less capital at risk than buying single assets.

docs.t: CLM-011092 data_ai
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: AI partnerships: Lilly (Isomorphic USD 45 million upfront, insitro, Chai), AbbVie (BigHat USD 30 million upfront) and Takeda (Nabla double-digit millions upfront, Iambic) all use milestone-heavy contracts with no disclosed candidate or independent outcome, so the exposure is mostly contingent.

docs.t: CLM-011093 robotics_automation
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Robotics and automation: Lilly divested its robotic lab to a CRO, J&J took a USD 0.9 billion impairment on Ottava (Auris), and Takeda has no disclosed automation programme; the evidenced working model is service procurement from CROs and cloud labs.

docs.t: CLM-011094 patient_care
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Clinical organisations and trial operations: J&J reports AI trial-site recommendation with up to 2.6x enrolment at better sites (self-reported pilot-level, no baseline) and Takeda lists Charles River as a collaborator; no independent trial-operations outcome from any partnership was found.

docs.t: CLM-011095 patient_care
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Health systems: J&J's OTTAVA trial ran at Memorial Hermann and Polyphonic is in early access at select hospitals, with Abu Dhabi deployment expected; Takeda has no disclosed health-system data network and its patient-services evidence is a gap.

docs.t: CLM-011096 data_ai
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Diagnostics and real-world data: Roche bought Flatiron for USD 1.9 billion in 2018 and kept it neutral; no comparable Takeda deal or registry was found in public sources, and Flatiron's regulatory-use claim is vendor marketing.

docs.t: CLM-011097 data_ai
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Data infrastructure: consortium and platform partners (Apheris for AISB, Benchling for TuneLab, Databricks for Takeda's agent platform) supply infrastructure without transferring data ownership; the AISB result is a vendor-organised benchmark that is not peer reviewed.

docs.t: CLM-011098 robotics_automation
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Manufacturing technology: Lilly bought a manufacturing site (NexPharm, USD 925 million) and announced a USD 4.5 billion Medicine Foundry; Takeda is expanding plasma fractionation in Los Angeles (USD 230 million) with no disclosed automation partner.

docs.t: CLM-011099 partnerships_ma
docs.x: INTERPRETATION: Venture funds and venture creation: Lilly runs Lilly Ventures inside Catalyze360, AbbVie Ventures has an unresolved founding date, J&J reportedly closed four JLABS sites, and Takeda's Center for External Innovation is on the BaseLaunch board with scope not public.

docs.t: CLM-000287 AbbVie financials
docs.x: AbbVie's balance-sheet non-current long-term debt and finance lease obligations were USD 58,941 million at 2025-12-31 (USD 60,340 million at 2024-12-31), compared with total long-term debt including the current portion of USD 64,503 million (XBRL us-gaap:LongTermDebt).

docs.t: CLM-000288 Johnson & Johnson financials
docs.x: Johnson & Johnson's balance-sheet long-term debt (Note 7, non-current) was USD 39,438 million at 2025-12-28 (USD 30,651 million at 2024-12-29), compared with total long-term debt including the current portion of USD 41,438 million (XBRL us-gaap:LongTermDebt).

docs.t: Answers to the ten comparison questions Competitor comparison: Lilly, J&J, AbbVie and the Takeda baseline
docs.x: 1. Why is Lilly winning where it wins? Revenue rose from USD 28.3bn to USD 65.2bn (FY2021-FY2025) [CLM-000133] [CLM-000137] because tirzepatide went from launch in 2022 to 56.0% of sales [CLM-001003]. Pre-tax margin rose from 21.7% to 39.5% [CLM-001007]. Capex rose from USD 1.3bn to USD 7.8bn [CLM-000168] [CLM-000172]. The evidenced mechanisms are a launched incretin with strong trial results, capacity built after a shortage, a cash-pay channel and a follow-on pipeline [CLM-001042] [CLM-001030]. Durability is not shown: realised prices fell 15% in Q3 2026 and about USD 900m of that quarter was one-off [CLM-014003]. (INTERPRETATION) Lilly is winning in a category where demand exceeded supply; the registry does not show the advantage persisting once supply and competition normalise. 2. What is distinctive about J&J's pharma and MedTech combination, and where is the synergy unevidenced? J&J is the only one of the four with a MedTech segment (USD 33.8bn beside Innovative Medicine USD 60.4bn) [CLM-000253]. MedTech grew 2.5% in Q3 2026 and J&J announced the Orthopaedics separation [CLM-002060] [CLM-002037]. J&J claims cardiovascular leadership; no cross-segment synergy is disclosed [CLM-002074]. The evidenced feature is diversification: the largest brand is 15.2% of revenue [CLM-002073]. Offsetting evidence: the Impella recall and the Varipulse pause [CLM-002046] [CLM-002044]. 3. How did AbbVie absorb the Humira loss of exclusivity? Global Humira fell from USD 21,237m (2022) to 4,540m (2025), -78.6% (computed) [CLM-003002]. Skyrizi plus Rinvoq rose by USD 18,179m against a Humira loss of 16,697m, and total revenue passed its 2022 peak only in 2025 [CLM-003014] [CLM-003015]. Three mechanisms are evidenced: successors already marketed and extended across Humira's indications [CLM-003084]; rebate-for-access contracting that held at least 97% of volume to March 2024 [CLM-003007]; and settlements putting Rinvoq entry no earlier than April 2037 [CLM-003021]. Steep U.S. declines (-41% in 2024, -57% in 2025) followed the April

docs.x: 2024 formulary change, an association rather than proven causation [CLM-003010]. 4. Who converts R&D into commercial outcomes best? No ranking is supported. R&D intensity moved from 24.5% to 20.5% at Lilly, held near 15.6% at J&J, rose from 12.6% to 14.9% at AbbVie and held 14.7-15.0% at Takeda (computed) [CLM-001006] [CLM-000085] [CLM-000015] [CLM-005004]. The share of FY2025 revenue from post-2021 molecules (Lilly at least 56.0%, J&J at least 3.2%, AbbVie at least 1.8%) is invalid as a productivity measure: it penalises lifecycle growth, mixes acquired and in-house assets, and Takeda is not computable [CLM-012013] [CLM-012014] [CLM-000270]. (INTERPRETATION) The narrow supportable statement is that Lilly's growth comes from a molecule approved inside the window and AbbVie's from molecules approved before it. 5. Who has the most defensible technology ecosystem? The registry cannot rank. Lilly has the largest evidenced build (LillyPod, TuneLab) with no outcome shown [CLM-006004] [CLM-000280] [CLM-006007]. J&J holds the only regulator records, and they concern devices [CLM-014022] [CLM-014026]. AbbVie has the ARCH knowledge graph [CLM-006032]. Takeda is partnership-led [CLM-006039] [CLM-006041]. (HYPOTHESIS) "Lilly is most defensible" rests on proprietary data the company estimates at over USD 1bn [CLM-000280] [CLM-006055]. 6. Which AI investments are operationally meaningful? docs.x: 524 sources, 1,401 claims, cutoff 2026-11-21. Numbers come from claim IDs in the claims registry, honouring correction fields; (computed) marks arithmetic on cited claims. Dossiers: Lilly, J&J, AbbVie, Takeda (all v1.1). Audit: Gate 1 passed Lilly, conditionally passed J&J and AbbVie, and failed Takeda as repairable with v1.1 repairs applied and a re-audit pending (verdicts). Independent corroboration is recorded on 2 of 1,401 claims, and 71 of 83 Takeda claims rest on a single interested source [CLM-000280] [CLM-005033].

docs.t: MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: Cutoff 2026-11-21. Takeda fiscal year (FY) 2025 = April 2025 to March 2026 [CLM-005000]. Takeda amounts stay in JPY. Every dollar figure for a strategic bet is an ASSUMPTION with an ID in the assumptions register; Takeda's own budget is not public (IVB-014). Challenge status. The Strategic Council (119 verdicts: 45 support, 64 conditional, 10 oppose), the red team and the stress test have run. The Director's decisions of 2026-11-21 are applied here as strategy v2 (decision record). The v1 strategy files have not yet been rewritten to match, so where they differ this summary says "v2 per Director decision record".

docs.t: 1. What is changing MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: Entyvio was JPY 958.0bn, 21% of FY2025 revenue [CLM-005009]. Takeda says it loses regulatory exclusivity in the latter half of the decade and that some patents expire in 2032 [CLM-005017] [CLM-014050]. Two biosimilar applications are under FDA review [CLM-014051]. CMS selected Entyvio for a negotiated Medicare price from January 2028 [CLM-007026]. CVS template formularies already prefer Stelara biosimilars [CLM-007015]. Vyvanse fell from JPY 423.2bn to 203.2bn in two years [CLM-005015]. Group revenue fell 1.7% (-2.7% at constant rates) in FY2025 [CLM-005001]. (SCENARIO, not a forecast) At the ASM-024 erosion range of 40-80% over three years, Entyvio revenue at risk is JPY 383-766bn a year. The base is global while first entry is a U.S. event, so the figure overstates the first three years [CLM-005012] (ASM-024).

docs.t: 2. Who is winning MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: Lilly's revenue rose from USD 28.3bn to USD 65.2bn between FY2021 and FY2025, with tirzepatide at 56.0% of sales [CLM-000133] [CLM-000137] [CLM-001003]. AbbVie replaced Humira (USD 21,237m to 4,540m) with Skyrizi plus Rinvoq (USD 7,687m to 25,866m) [CLM-003002] [CLM-003014]. J&J absorbed a 41.3% Stelara decline with its largest brand at 15.2% of revenue [CLM-000254] [CLM-002073]. Rankings on new-molecule revenue share or approvals per R&D dollar are not used because the audit marks them invalid [CLM-012013] [CLM-000270].

docs.t: 3. Why MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: (INTERPRETATION) Winning here means a successor already marketed before the cliff [CLM-003084], capacity built ahead of demand (Lilly capex USD 7,841m in FY2025) [CLM-000172], and a diversified base. It does not yet mean AI: no independent outcome exists for any company's AI programme [CLM-011052] [CLM-006054, wording stronger than its sources support per audit]. Durability is open: Lilly's realised prices fell 15% in Q3 2026 and about USD 900m of that quarter was one-off [CLM-014003].

docs.t: 4. What is defensible MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: (INTERPRETATION) Compute and third-party models can be bought; proprietary decision-linked data, built capacity and clinical execution cannot [CLM-006055] [CLM-011085]. Infrastructure, IP and workflow moats are best evidenced and each is removable: announced capacity is not operating capacity, patents expire, PBM templates change [CLM-007015]. (HYPOTHESIS) Lilly's data position is the most defensible of the four; the registry has no outcome to confirm it [CLM-000280].

docs.t: 5. What Takeda already has MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: A plasma network of more than 270 centres with adaptive nomograms and a USD 230m Los Angeles fractionation expansion [CLM-005060] [CLM-005065]. In-house orexin science that produced an FDA approval on 2026-08-05 [CLM-005048] [CLM-005029]. Rusfertide approved 2026-08-28 and a zasocitinib NDA accepted under Priority Review [CLM-005032] [CLM-005035]. Three Phase 3 readouts delivered positive on the 2024 plan [CLM-005042]. Stop discipline, including a JPY 58.2bn cell-therapy impairment [CLM-009084]. Deal flow: Nimbus USD 4.0bn upfront, Innovent USD 1.2bn upfront [CLM-009076] [CLM-009078]. Constraints: leverage 2.6x at March 2026, the Amitiza provision of JPY 403.5bn, a CEO in post since 24 June 2026 and three launches in twelve months [CLM-005005] [CLM-005014] [CLM-005073] [CLM-005074]. AI outcomes, lab automation and patient services are public-evidence gaps, not proven absences [CLM-005080] [CLM-005067] [CLM-005072].

docs.t: 6. Where the opportunity is MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: (RECOMMENDATION) In order of evidence strength: (1) defend and extend the dated Entyvio exposure (BET-04, BET-11); (2) back the replacement set already in hand (BET-05); (3) compound the two strengths no peer in the set shares, plasma process data and orexin biology (BET-02, BET-03); (4) buy licences for Phase 2/3 assets, the instrument Takeda has actually used (BET-18); (5) hold capped options on AI and new modalities (BET-06 to BET-09); (6) build the measurement discipline that makes AI claims testable (BET-01, BET-17, BET-12).

docs.t: 10. How to measure MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: (RECOMMENDATION) Set baselines before claims: AI use cases with owner, baseline and measured benefit (usage and training counts are not value [CLM-014043]); yield and cost per litre at the plasma pilot; time to first dose and persistence for launches; Entyvio net price and persistence by payer segment; option conversion and impairment share; revenue concentration against the Entyvio-era 21% [CLM-005009]. Measurement ownership moves off the CFO, who owns the JPY 200bn savings target [CLM-005059].

docs.t: Reader notes MEDICINE 2040: executive summary for Takeda
docs.x: CEO. (RECOMMENDATION) Treat Entyvio as a dated defence plus a refill problem. The evidence supports that reading over a platform story. Fund the defence and the replacement set, keep AI and new modalities as capped options with stop rules, and decline three expensive alternatives (owned lab, model platform, U.S. cash-pay) where the record shows divestment, distressed sale or poor fit [CLM-006052] [CLM-006051] [CLM-007052]. Execution load is high. CFO. (ASSUMPTION) Capital is a range, not a plan. The two binding variables are leverage and Amitiza cash timing (IVB-012). Contingent payments in AI and option deals exceed USD 1bn on single deals and cost nothing without data [CLM-006039] [CLM-006041]. No NPV is reported because it would need internal forecasts (IVB-004, IVB-005). AbbVie wrote off 54% of the Cerevel net price [CLM-009054]. R&D leader. (RECOMMENDATION) Refill after 2030 depends on early depth that is not public (IVB-008). Fund orexin at USD 300m with a Phase 1 gate and an additionality test against base R&D. Gate CNS assets on Phase 2 quality; neuroscience assets failed at AbbVie, J&J and Takeda [CLM-003054] [CLM-002039] [CLM-012120]. Rent wet-lab automation [CLM-006013]. CTO. (RECOMMENDATION) Extend the existing agent platform with governance and a decision log; do not build a rival [CLM-005058]. Models converge, so the moat is Takeda's own decision-linked data [CLM-006056] [CLM-006055]. Document model credibility against FDA's January 2025 draft framework [CLM-006046]. Commercial leader. (RECOMMENDATION) Build payer-contracting depth before January 2028 [CLM-007026]. Humira held at least 97% of volume to March 2024 and still lost 78.6% in three years, so contracting delays erosion rather than preventing it [CLM-003007] [CLM-003002]. Resolve whether subcutaneous conversion helps or hurts after entry (BET-04 and BET-11 conflict) [CLM-007053]. Launch pathways attach to the oveporexton launch. docs.t: 1. What to do first (next 12 months, to 2027 H2) Recommendations
docs.x: 1. Close the dated Entyvio questions first (BET-04). Entyvio is JPY 958.0bn, 21% of revenue, with Medicare negotiation effective January 2028 and two biosimilar applications under FDA review [CLM-005009] [CLM-007026] [CLM-014051]. In 2027 H1 approve erosion scenarios and the patent posture, and run the benefit-channel gate (IVB-004): what share of Entyvio volume sits in the contractable pharmacy channel. The registry has no medical-versus-pharmacy split [CLM-003007]. If most volume sits outside it, redirect part of the USD 140m to provider and site-of-care strategy. Set the target as "delay and measure net price and persistence", not "retain 10 points". Have the biosimilar-event playbook live by 2028 H1 (v2 per Director decision record; was 2029 H2). 2. Back the replacement set already in hand (BET-05). Zasocitinib NDA is accepted under Priority Review, and the PsA Phase 3 completes in May 2027 [CLM-005035] [CLM-005037]. Fund breadth and comparative evidence at USD 180m, and measure payer coverage at 6 and 12 months after launch. 3. Open the Phase 2/3 licensing channel (BET-18, new in v2). Takeda's approved late-stage set came mostly from licences, and the channel has no funding in v1 [CLM-005050] [CLM-009076] [CLM-009078]. Set a per-deal upfront ceiling of USD 0.5-2bn, tie release to IVB-012 (Amitiza cash) and the 3.0x leverage ceiling (ASM-033), and complete its design template in A11c-bis. 4. Run the plasma baseline, not the roll-out (BET-02, now EXPERIMENT). Measure yield, cost per litre and deviations across a sample of centres and Los Angeles (IVB-006). Test whether plasma is demand-bound or capacity-bound: PDT revenue was -1.5% at constant rates in H1 FY2026 [CLM-005064]. Re-base the 2% pass mark (ASM-031) on money before releasing the roughly USD 365m remainder. 5. Start measurement before value claims (BET-17, BET-01). Inventory AI and data products with owner and baseline (IVB-001, IVB-003). Adopt a thin-slice data standard

docs.t: 2. What to avoid Recommendations
docs.x: - A USD 5bn+ asset purchase (BET-15, REJECT as framed in v2). The council's arithmetic gives 3.13x leverage after the purchase and 3.41x if the Amitiza provision is also debt-funded, against a 3.0x planning ceiling; free cash flow is ignored [CLM-005005] [CLM-005014]. - An owned autonomous lab (BET-10, zero spend). Owned and venture-funded lab models ended in divestment or distressed sale [CLM-006052] [CLM-006051]. Revisit only if three triggers fire: an independent Lilly-lab result, Nabla first-in-human data, a measured CRO cost [CLM-011066] [CLM-000281]. - A TuneLab-style model platform (BET-14). The public record shows no measured Takeda advantage and no external demand [CLM-000280]. - A U.S. cash-pay channel (BET-16). The channel fits infused and specialty-distributed products poorly [CLM-007052]. - Scaling subcutaneous and device spend (BET-11) before baselining it. SC moves patients into the pharmacy benefit, where PBM biosimilar templates operate; persistence after entry is unestablished [CLM-007015] [CLM-007053]. - Redesigning patient programmes without a pilot: AbbVie reversed its loyalty redesign within months [CLM-003033]. - Reading the USD 10-20bn peak range for six late-stage programmes as a forecast; it is not probability-adjusted [CLM-014049]. - Funding the registry (BET-13) now. The v2 carry is removed; a USD 25m options paper is funded from BET-12 in 2029 (RM-028).

docs.t: 3. How to decide whether to scale Recommendations
docs.x: Decide on the evidence listed at each gate, against a baseline set at the preceding gate, never on spend to date. A missed stop criterion ends or redirects the bet unless the decision authority records a reason in writing. Expansion releases only the next tranche (stage gates.md). Bet Scale only if Stop or redirect if --- --- --- BET-01 Measured effect in at least one decision; reuse above the threshold set at feasibility No attributable benefit in two consecutive annual reviews BET-02 Shadow-mode predictions beat the nomogram baseline [CLM-005060]; pilot at or above the re-based threshold with clean inspection No vendor accepts outcome-linked terms; new inspection observations from the pilot [CLM-005020] BET-03 Clean Phase 1 for a second candidate; Phase 2 design with credible placebo response Safety or exposure failure; platform claim withdrawn if only one asset by 2040 BET-04 Pilot retains share; retained share above the scenario midpoint Retained share below the scenario low case: redirect to lifecycle BET-05 PsA positive; payer coverage at plan PsA misses primary endpoint; coverage below plan BET-06 Conversion at or above 0.10 (ASM-028); fees within band Conversion below 0.05; impairments above the 54% benchmark [CLM-009054] BET-07 Data positive and Phase 2 transition at or above conventional Data absent by 2028 H2 or negative; success-based payments grow faster than data BET-11 Persistence higher than IV after entry SC erodes net price faster than it retains patients BET-18 Leverage at or below ASM-033 after IVB-012; Phase 2 or later data; write-down test passed Any trigger unmet

docs.t: 4. Measurable success metrics Recommendations
docs.x: (ASSUMPTION targets; Takeda sets the values.) Metrics and the year each is first read: - 2028: inventory of AI and data products with owner, baseline and measured benefit; Entyvio contracting posture and playbook in place (BET-17, BET-01, BET-04). - 2029: plasma pilot result against the re-based threshold; AI-partnership decision made on data; checkpoint on the JPY 200bn savings plan with the technology share disclosed internally [CLM-005059]. - 2032: plasma network status; options exercised; share of Entyvio exposure replaced by labelled indications (BET-02, BET-06, BET-05). - 2035: first option-sourced approval check; decisions changed by models with measured effect (BET-06, BET-01). - 2040: revenue concentration against the Entyvio-era 21% [CLM-005009]. - Always: time to first dose and persistence for launches; Entyvio net price and persistence by payer segment; option conversion and impairment share; cost per data point against the internal baseline. Usage and training counts are not outcomes [CLM-006022] [CLM-014043].

docs.t: 2. The seven transformation domains Takeda strategy 2027-2040 (strategy v2)
docs.x: Each domain states the problem, what competitors show, and Takeda's position. Sources: strategy/future of pharma. 1. Data advantage. Proprietary data is the one input rivals cannot buy [CLM-006055]. AbbVie built ARCH with fewer than ten full-time staff and opened data from 2,000+ trials to all R&D [CLM-006032] [CLM-006034]; Lilly's TuneLab rests on data it estimates cost over USD 1bn [CLM-000280]. None has independent outcome evidence [CLM-011052]. Takeda has an agent platform and 63.4% workforce usage, both adoption measures [CLM-005058] [CLM-014043]. (RECOMMENDATION) BET-01 and BET-08. 2. Next-generation R&D. Every competitor AI-discovery deal found is at concept or prototype [CLM-011057]. Takeda's Nabla and Iambic collaborations carry success-based payments above USD 1bn and USD 1.7bn, payable only on data [CLM-006039] [CLM-006041]. AI-origin Phase 2 success is cited as about the same as conventional (secondary source) [CLM-006049]. Takeda's approved late-stage set is mostly licensed in, with orexin the in-house exception [CLM-005050] [CLM-005048]. (RECOMMENDATION) BET-03, BET-06, BET-07, BET-18. 3. Robotics and autonomous science. Scripted automation is a commodity service: Arctoris runs the former Lilly platform as a CRO [CLM-006013] [CLM-006016]. Owned or venture-funded labs ended in divestment or distressed sale [CLM-006052] [CLM-006051]. (INTERPRETATION) The Lilly-NVIDIA lab (up to USD 1bn, joint) can also be read as re-platforming at larger scale, so "owned labs fail" is weaker than first stated [CLM-000281] [CLM-006017]. (RECOMMENDATION) BET-09 rents; BET-10 stays at zero with triggers. 4. Care models. No company publishes adherence, persistence or time-to-therapy outcomes; reported figures are enrolment or access counts [CLM-007039]. Entyvio SC is approved in three regions and Takeda cites it as driving uptake; HYHUB received 510(k) clearance [CLM-007041] [CLM-007042]. Effect after biosimilar entry is unestablished [CLM-007053]. (RECOMMENDATION) BET-11, BET-12. 5. Commercial models. PBM template formularies decide biosimilar outcomes [CLM-007015]. Humira's contracting delayed but did not stop erosion [CLM-003007] [CLM-003002]. Takeda's contracting and patient-services evidence is

docs.t: 4. Sequencing logic Takeda strategy 2027-2040 (strategy v2)
docs.x: (HYPOTHESIS argued from evidence) Run the data standard and rented automation in parallel from 2027 H1, with a hard gate before any closed-loop (stage 3) work: the full data layer plus three triggers (an independent Lilly-lab result, Nabla first-in-human data, a measured CRO cost) [CLM-011066] [CLM-000281] [CLM-006039]. Plasma can seed its own data because nomogram data already exist at site level [CLM-005060]. The Entyvio chain has fixed dates and cannot slip: erosion scenarios, then the January 2028 posture, then the playbook live by 2028 H1 (v2), then the earliest entry window (ASM-025 widened to 2028-2032 in v2), then the 2032 patents [CLM-007026] [CLM-014051] [CLM-005017]. Licensing deals (BET-18) wait for IVB-012 and the leverage test.

docs.t: 5. What Takeda should not do Takeda strategy 2027-2040 (strategy v2)
docs.x: (RECOMMENDATION) Do not buy a USD 5bn+ asset on current leverage (BET-15). Do not build an owned autonomous lab (BET-10) or a TuneLab-style platform (BET-14). Do not launch a U.S. cash-pay channel (BET-16). Do not scale AI-design partnerships before first-in-human data (RM-020, 2028 H2). Do not roll out plasma automation before the baseline shows headroom (ASM-031). Do not read usage or training counts as value [CLM-014043] [CLM-006022]. Do not redesign patient programmes without a pilot: AbbVie reversed its loyalty redesign within months [CLM-003033]. Do not treat the USD 10-20bn peak range for six late-stage programmes as a forecast; it is not probability-adjusted [CLM-014049].

docs.t: 6. Where the strategy is weakest Takeda strategy 2027-2040 (strategy v2)
docs.x: (INTERPRETATION) The council rates no funded bet robust to pricing and biosimilar pressure (SCN-3). The Entyvio price from January 2028 is statutory and PBM private-label biosimilars route around contracts, so BET-04 holds value only as delay [CLM-007026] [CLM-007015]. Vyvanse, Trintellix and Takhzyro (patent to January 2036) are exposures the bets do not address [CLM-005015] [CLM-005016] [CLM-005019]. The probabilities behind the ranking (ASM-020, 021, 022, 028) are judgment.

docs.t: 1. Executive thesis AbbVie Inc. — master dossier v1.1 (A3, cutoff 2026-11-21)
docs.x: AbbVie absorbed the largest U.S. loss of exclusivity in pharma by replacing Humira (global USD 21.2bn in 2022 to 4.5bn in 2025) with Skyrizi and Rinvoq (7.7bn to 25.9bn) [CLM-003002, CLM-003014]. Total revenue dipped 6.4% in 2023 and passed its 2022 peak only in 2025 (61.2bn) [CLM-003015]. The immunology engine is high quality; the diversification layer is mixed: emraclidine failed and cost a USD 4.5bn impairment [CLM-003057], aesthetics shrank [CLM-003031], while Vyalev, Elahere and Juvmo are real but small [CLM-003037, CLM-003036, CLM-003063].

docs.t: 20. Capability Mechanism Cards (INTERPRETATION) AbbVie Inc. — master dossier v1.1 (A3, cutoff 2026-11-21)
docs.x: Card 1: successor sequencing. Problem: 37% of revenue exposed to LOE. Built/bought: Skyrizi/Rinvoq expanded across Humira indications, plus head-to-head data. Enablers: immunology sales force, IL-23/JAK science. Outcome: 25.9bn in 2025. Replicate: launch the successor 3-5 years before the cliff [CLM-003084, CLM-003016]. Card 2: contracting defence. Problem: biosimilar entry. Mechanism: rebate-for-access kept =97% volume to March 2024, then co-branded Humira via Cordavis took 23% of switchers vs 60% for co-promoted Hyrimoz. Limit: 2025 U.S. -57% [CLM-003085]. Card 3: BD&L refill. Problem: pipeline gap. Mechanism: buy late-stage/commercial assets (18.5bn consideration transferred in 2024 for ImmunoGen and Cerevel; 17.5bn net of cash acquired). Outcome: one 4.5bn write-down, Elahere growth, Juvmo approval; returns not yet demonstrated [CLM-003086]. Card 4: settlement-based IP. Rinvoq entry deferred to 2037 after 2025 settlements; Humira history unverified [CLM-003087]. Card 5: aesthetics channel (risk). Loyalty redesign cut share and price; reversed within months [CLM-003033, CLM-003088].

docs.t: Moats (INTERPRETATION, A3) Moats (INTERPRETATION, A3)

Contracting and lifecycle/IP strategy: [CLM-003085, CLM-003087, CLM-003021]; Humira settlement licence-start years (2023 U.S., 2018 Europe) are now sourced; terms remain undisclosed [CLM-014036]. 3. Single-interested-source note: moat 2 rests on trade-sourced contracting figures [CLM-003085].

docs.x: 1. Incretin manufacturing scale. Facts: [CLM-001038] [CLM-001039] [CLM-001041] [CLM-001023]. (INTERPRETATION) Mechanism: multi-year, multi-billion API and device capacity; rival replication needs 3-5 years and capital; announced capacity is not operating capacity (operating evidence only at Concord, Kinsale, Lebanon Advanced Therapies: [CLM-014014] [CLM-014011] [CLM-014015]). 2. Oral GLP-1 timing. Facts: [CLM-001030] [CLM-001058]. (INTERPRETATION) Small-molecule pill avoids peptide supply limits; ATTAIN-1 weight loss is below injectable tirzepatide; rivals have oral peptide products. 3. Proprietary preclinical data (TuneLab) [CLM-000280]: operational platform, no outcome or revenue evidence (maturity: operational, unproven value); partner uptake unquantified [CLM-014056]. 4. Compute partnership [CLM-000281] [CLM-000282]: concept stage. 5. Patent runway: tirzepatide compound patent 2036 [CLM-000250].

docs.t: 1. Executive thesis Johnson & Johnson — master dossier (v1.1)
docs.x: J&J is the only one of the three comparator companies with two operating segments after separating Consumer Health: Innovative Medicine (USD 60.4bn, +6.0%) and MedTech (USD 33.8bn) in FY2025 [CLM-000253]. Its distinctive FY2025 outcome is absorbing the largest loss of exclusivity in its portfolio: STELARA fell 41.3% to USD 6.1bn [CLM-000254] while DARZALEX (USD 14.4bn) [CLM-000255], TREMFYA [CLM-000256] and CARVYKTI [CLM-000257] grew, and group sales still rose 6.0% [CLM-000253]. Excluding STELARA, sales grew about 12%, about 1 point acquired [CLM-002075] (INTERPRETATION) . The cost was debt: net debt rose to USD 27.8bn [CLM-002014]. Vulnerabilities: talc [CLM-002062], DARZALEX concentration [CLM-002073], MedTech margin and growth [CLM-002004] [CLM-002060].

docs.t: Moats (INTERPRETATION; mechanism and replication path) Moats (INTERPRETATION; mechanism and replication path)
docs.x: 1. Myeloma franchise depth. Mechanism: CD38 antibody, BCMA CAR-T, two bispecifics in one commercial organisation; USD 17.4bn in 2025 [CLM-002072]. Replication: multi-year clinical programmes plus cell-therapy manufacturing; erosion risk from DARZALEX concentration [CLM-002073]. Confidence: medium. 2. Pharma + MedTech dual platform. Mechanism claimed by J&J: cardiovascular leadership across Abiomed, Biosense Webster and Shockwave [CLM-002074]. No disclosed cross-segment revenue synergy; the margin gap and the Orthopaedics separation point the other way [CLM-002004] [CLM-002037]. Confidence: low (HYPOTHESIS). 3. Immunology scale and successor sequencing. Mechanism: TREMFYA and ICOTYDE as IL-23 successors with Crohn's/UC trials [CLM-002055] [CLM-002053]. Replication: requires an IL-23 asset launched 3–5 years pre-LOE. Confidence: medium; Immunology still fell 11.8% [CLM-002026]. 4. M&A bridge capacity. USD 17.5bn in 2025 alone, funded by debt [CLM-002013] [CLM-002014]; replicable by any well-capitalised peer. 5. JLABS/JJDC ecosystem. Contracting rather than expanding: JLABS planned at six sites with capacity for 225 companies in 2016 [CLM-009051]; Toronto, Houston and Washington D.C. exited, 11 sites in August 2025 [CLM-014064]; New York closure is a snippet [CLM-014065]. J&J claims more than 150 partnerships [CLM-009050]; no JJDC portfolio count or fund size found [CLM-014066]. Not evidenced as a moat (gap) . 6. Surgical robotics option. FDA records exist for OTTAVA (De Novo), MONARCH and VELYS [CLM-014022] [CLM-014025] [CLM-014026], but no installed base or procedure volume; OTTAVA has one announced installation site [CLM-000284]. Confidence: low (INTERPRETATION) .

docs.t: Top successes Successes and failures
docs.x: 1. DARZALEX USD 14,351m in FY2025 from 6,023m in FY2021 [CLM-002023]; myeloma brands total USD 17.4bn [CLM-002072]. 2. Absorbing the Stelara loss: group sales +6.0% in FY2025 with Stelara -41.3% [CLM-000254] [CLM-002075]. 3. CARVYKTI USD 1,887m (+95.9%) [CLM-000257] and bispecifics TECVAYLI 670 / TALVEY 463 [CLM-002024]. 4. Kenvue separation executed in two steps in 2023 with a USD 21.0bn gain [CLM-002006] [CLM-002007]. 5. Shockwave and Abiomed integration: Shockwave 1,146m in FY2025; Abiomed 1,751m (+17.1%) [CLM-002011] [CLM-002027]; ICOTYDE approval [CLM-002065]. 6. Intra-Cellular: CAPLYTA MDD approved in Q4 2025, nine months after the USD 14.5bn close; Momenta delivered IMAAVY (2025-04-30) [CLM-009030] [CLM-009031] [CLM-009044]. 7. Regulatory firsts in devices: OTTAVA De Novo [CLM-014022]; MONARCH and VELYS 510(k) clearances [CLM-014025] [CLM-014026].

docs.t: Failures and weaknesses Successes and failures
docs.x: 1. Talc: three bankruptcy attempts, two dismissed (LTL 2021, 2023), Red River not confirmed 2025-03-31; USD ~7.0bn charge in FY2023 and ~5.0bn in 2024 [CLM-002015] [CLM-002016] [CLM-002017] [CLM-002043]; 2026 proposed USD 5.5bn+ resolution [CLM-002062] [CLM-002063]. 2. Aticaprant Phase 3 stopped for insufficient efficacy [CLM-002039] [CLM-002056]. 3. RSV adult vaccine and infectious-disease exits [CLM-002018]; COVID-19 vaccine exit costs USD 1.5bn [CLM-002019]. 4. Bermekimab write-off ~USD 0.8bn [CLM-002020]. 5. Varipulse U.S. pause: 4 of 132 patients with stroke/TIA vs ≤1% expected [CLM-002044] [CLM-002045]; PFA competition [CLM-002028]. 6. Impella Class I recalls: 66,390 pumps, 129 serious injuries incl. 49 deaths (IFU correction); controller purge-retainer recall 2025 [CLM-002046] [CLM-002047]. 7. Stelara cliff and Orthopaedics at 1.1% growth [CLM-002022] [CLM-002029]; IRA price negotiation [CLM-002054]. 8. docs.t: Established LOE exposure and revenue-replacement logic
docs.x: - VYVANSE/ELVANSE: JPY 423.2bn (FY2023) to 350.6bn to 203.2bn (FY2025). U.S. composition-of-matter patent and pediatric exclusivity expired August 2023; Takeda expects the decline to continue in FY2026 [CLM-005015]. - AZILVA fell to JPY 7.1bn after a February 2023 Japanese generic approval. TRINTELLIX (JPY 121.8bn) faces generics after certain patent rights expire in December 2026 [CLM-005016]. - ENTYVIO (JPY 958.0bn, 21% of revenue): regulatory exclusivity ends in the latter half of the decade; some patents expire in 2032; biosimilar timing is uncertain [CLM-005017]. Disclosed defences: subcutaneous Pen and pediatric labels [CLM-005018]. H1 FY2026 ENTYVIO growth is +2.7% at constant rates [CLM-005012]. - TAKHZYRO U.S. patent is listed to January 2036; no U.S. generic of GATTEX had launched by March 2026 [CLM-005019]. - Leuprorelin: the Hikari supply disruption produced a USD 505m award to AbbVie [CLM-005020]. - Velcade history was not examined (gap) .

docs.t: Successes Takeda: successes and failures, November 2021 to November 2026
docs.x: 1. Three novel FDA approvals in the window : Fruzaqla 2023-11-08 [CLM-012018]; Orzeyful (oveporexton, narcolepsy type 1) 2026-08-05 [CLM-012019]; Mimrylo (rusfertide, polycythemia vera) 2026-08-28 [CLM-012020] [CLM-005029] [CLM-005032]. The zasocitinib NDA was accepted with Priority Review on 2026-09-14 [CLM-005035]; the R&D Day plan was met for the first three assets by November 2026 [CLM-005042]. 2. ENTYVIO subcutaneous conversion : SC pen approved for UC (September 2023) and Crohn's disease (April 2024) and described as driving uptake [CLM-007033] [CLM-007041] [CLM-005018]; ENTYVIO JPY 958.0bn, 21% of revenue, +2.7% at constant rates in H1 FY2026 [CLM-007027] [CLM-005012]. 3. Growth & Launch Products reached 51% of revenue in FY2025 (43% in FY2023) [CLM-005008]; QDENGA JPY 40.8bn [CLM-005045]. 4. Plasma network and operations : 233 to 275 centres over FY2022-FY2024; 99.6% on-time in-full in FY2025 [CLM-005063] [CLM-014046]. 5. Portfolio discipline : stopped programmes early (TAK-994, soticlestat, cell therapy) while Core Operating Profit stayed near JPY 1.05-1.19 trillion [CLM-005023] [CLM-005024] [CLM-005025] [CLM-005003] (INTERPRETATION) .

docs.t: Failures and weaknesses Takeda: successes and failures, November 2021 to November 2026
docs.x: 1. TAK-994 : Phase 2 stopped in 2021 for a liver-related safety signal and not developed further (decision June 2022); the Phase 3 pevonedistat MDS trial missed its event-free-survival endpoint [CLM-012119] [CLM-005023]. 2. EXKIVITY withdrawn globally (October 2023) after EXCLAIM-2 missed its primary endpoint; JPY 28.5bn impairment [CLM-012121] [CLM-012122] [CLM-005022]. 3. ALOFISEL : JPY 74.0bn impairment after the Phase 3 ADMIRE-CD II topline [CLM-012122]. 4. Soticlestat : Phase 3 SKYLINE and SKYWAY missed primary endpoints (June 2024); no filing; JPY 21.5bn impairment; discontinued January 2025 [CLM-012120] [CLM-009083] [CLM-005024]. 5. Cell therapy exit : all cell-therapy efforts discontinued on 2025-10-01; expected impairment JPY 58.0bn, recognised JPY 58.2bn on the gamma delta T-cell platform plus JPY 31.9bn on ALUNBRIG in the FY2025 20-F [CLM-005025] [CLM-009084] [CLM-012123]. 6. AMITIZA verdict : jury verdict of 2026-05-18 for USD 884.9m single damages (subject to trebling for two groups); JPY 403.5bn provision; reported FY2025 operating profit JPY 6.2bn; Takeda intends post-trial motions and an appeal; final judgment amount and post-trial status unverified [CLM-005013] [CLM-005014] [CLM-014048] [CLM-014047]. 7. VYVANSE loss of exclusivity : JPY 423.2bn (FY2023) to 203.2bn (FY2025); TRINTELLIX generics expected after December 2026 [CLM-005015] [CLM-005016]. 8. Partnership terminations : Denali collaboration ended April 2026; Neurocrine terminated TAK-041 and TAK-831 (March 2025); TAK-004 discontinued (single secondary source) [CLM-009089] [CLM-009090] [CLM-005026]. 9. Manufacturing quality : the 2020 Hikari warning letter led to a leuprorelin shortage and a USD 505m award to AbbVie (Delaware court, December 2023) [CLM-005020]. 10. Teva Takeda Pharma JV dissolved with a JPY 18.9bn impairment [CLM-009085].

docs.t: 1.1 Price versus volume in the growth years Commercial capabilities comparison
docs.x: Lilly's 2025 revenue growth came from volume, partly offset by lower realised prices, mostly on Mounjaro and Zepbound. In Q4 2025 realised prices were 5% lower and volume 46% higher; in Q3 2026 realised prices were 15% lower and volume 53% higher, and the quarter included about USD 900m of one-off benefits (USD 410m of Jardiance milestones plus rebate and discount estimate adjustments) [CLM-007024] [CLM-014004] [CLM-014003]. J&J's Stelara decline cut Innovative Medicine growth by about 10.4 points in FY2025 [CLM-007017]. AbbVie's reported provisions for rebates and chargebacks (USD 65.1bn in 2025, 59.3bn in 2024, 56.8bn in 2023) show the scale of its gross-to-net, which none of the other three companies disclose in the sources read [CLM-007019].
